found.title: The Plover Who Fought the Ocean (the tittibha couple)
found.source_ref: Panchatantra Book 1 (The Loss of Friends / Mitrabheda). In Ryder (1925), the jackal Victor (Damanaka) tells it to the bull Lively (Sanjivaka) to talk him out of a fight: 'He loses fights who fights before / His foeman's power is reckoned' (Ryder approx. pp. 145-162). Sanskrit check (IGNCA edition): katha 12 'tittibha-dampati-katha', verse 337 'satror vikramam ajnatva vairam arabhate hi yah | sa parabhavam apnoti samudram tittibhad yatha'. The bird is the Sanskrit ṭiṭṭibha (a lapwing or sandpiper), the same word as in Tittibhasana.
found.story_plain: A plover couple lives on the seashore. When it is time to lay her eggs, the wife asks to move, because the ocean's tide might reach the nest and take her babies. The husband laughs and says the ocean knows him and would never dare. The ocean overhears, waits until both birds are out looking for food, and takes the eggs with a wave. The plover calls all the birds. They beat the sea with their wings and try to fill it with dust, then ask an old gander, who sends them to Garuda, king of birds. Garuda refuses Vishnu's summons until the wrong is put right, so Vishnu comes himself, fits a fire-arrow to his bow and orders the ocean to give the eggs back, and the ocean returns them, trembling.
found.key_quote: "Oh," said she, "don't mention this dreadful place. Here is the ocean near at hand. His tide might someday make a long reach and lick away my babies." But the plover answered: "Sweetheart, he knows me, he knows Sprawl. Surely the great ocean cannot show such enmity to me."
found.safety_notes: Leave out the frame story: in it a scheming jackal is manipulating a bull and a lion king at court. In Ryder the wife says she has 'decided to burn myself'. That is a self-harm line, so do not use it. Ryder also writes 'rape of his chicks' in the old sense of 'seizure'. Say 'stolen' instead. Garuda has been called to a 'battle between gods and demons', which is far in the background and fine to leave out. Treat Vishnu and Garuda with respect. Many studios call Tittibhasana 'firefly pose', but Sanskrit dictionaries (Apte, Monier-Williams via wisdomlib) give ṭiṭṭibha as a bird. Say 'lapwing/plover bird' and do not argue about the firefly name. Recensions differ: the Sanskrit IGNCA text has a different set of inner verses from Ryder's.
found.fit_note: This is the closest fit to today. The wife reads the water and wants to move before it rises, while the husband's pride ('the ocean knows me') costs them the eggs. Good fear here means respecting water you cannot control. The asana carries the bird's name. Bonus line from the same story, which the ocean says about the proud bird: 'The plover lies with claws upstretched / To prop the falling sky' (Ryder). The Sanskrit is 'utkṣipya ṭiṭṭibhaḥ pādāv āste bhaṅga-bhayād divaḥ': the bird lies with legs up for fear the sky will break. Dictionaries record this as a folk belief about the bird. That gives a second fear joke: the bird that thinks it holds up the sky. Help in getting the eggs back came from all the birds, then the old gander's advice, then Garuda, then Vishnu.
found.translation_used: Arthur W. Ryder, The Panchatantra (University of Chicago Press, 1925), public domain. Transcription by Laura Gibbs.

found.title: Forethought, Ready-Wit, and Fatalist (the three fish)
found.source_ref: Panchatantra Book 1, a story inside 'The Plover Who Fought the Ocean'. Constance, the plover wife, tells it to her husband Sprawl after he refuses to move the nest. Her point is that the one who leaves things to fate dies. He answers: 'My dear, why do you think me like Fatalist?' Sanskrit (IGNCA edition, katha 14 'anagata-vidhatadi-matsya-traya-katha'): the fish are Anāgatavidhātā (Forethought), Pratyutpannamati (Ready-wit) and Yadbhaviṣya ('what will be', Ryder's Fatalist), and the female ṭiṭṭibhī tells it there too.
found.story_plain: Three big fish live in a lake: Forethought, Ready-wit and Fatalist. Forethought hears fishermen on the bank say they will come fishing tomorrow, and asks the other two to move with him to a quieter lake. Ready-wit says he has lived there a long time and will think of something if the fishermen come. Fatalist says one should not leave the lake of one's birth over gossip. Forethought leaves alone. Next day the nets catch every fish. Ready-wit plays dead, is laid on the bank, and wriggles back into the water, but Fatalist struggles in the net and is killed.
found.key_quote: Forethought and Ready-wit thrive; / Fatalist can't keep alive.
found.safety_notes: Fatalist is clubbed to death in the net. Keep it as 'caught' and do not show it. Recensions differ: in Ryder, Ready-wit stays and plays dead, while in the Sanskrit IGNCA text Ready-wit leaves with Forethought. Follow Ryder if you quote Ryder. Matsyasana has no textual link to these fish, so the connection is a theme only. Do not call Fatalist 'stupid' in a way that mocks people who cannot leave home in a flood (many cannot).
found.fit_note: This maps straight onto a rain warning. The weather report is the fishermen's talk on the bank. Rushing home early is Forethought, staying calm if you get caught is Ready-wit, and shrugging it off is Fatalist. It sits inside the plover story, so one reel can use both: the wife tells it to warn her proud husband. The Ready-wit line works for the mat too: 'I will protect myself by some means devised for the occasion.'
found.translation_used: Arthur W. Ryder, The Panchatantra (1925), public domain. Transcription by Laura Gibbs.

found.title: Manu and the small fish that warns of the flood
found.tradition: Vedic (Brahmana prose), the earliest Indian flood story
found.source_ref: Shatapatha Brahmana 1.8.1.1-6 (Kanda I, adhyaya 8, brahmana 1). In the Brahmana the fish is not named. Later Puranas identify it as Matsya, Vishnu's fish avatar.
found.story_plain: One morning, as Manu washes, a small fish comes into his hands and says: rear me, and I will save you from a flood that will carry away all creatures. Because small fish get eaten by bigger ones, Manu keeps it first in a jar, then in a pit, then takes it to the sea as it grows. The fish tells him the year the flood will come and tells him to prepare a ship. In that year Manu makes the ship ready. When the water rises the fish swims up, Manu ties the ship's rope to its horn, and he is carried to the northern mountain. The fish tells him to tie the ship to a tree and come down slowly as the water goes down, so that he is not cut off. Manu comes down gradually.
found.key_quote: It then said, 'I have saved thee. Fasten the ship to a tree; but let not the water cut thee off, whilst thou art on the mountain. As the water subsides, thou mayest gradually descend!'
found.safety_notes: In the myth the flood sweeps away every creature except Manu. Do not compare it to real Bangkok floods (such as 2011) or to any real disaster with victims. Keep the story about the warning and the patience. Paragraph 7 onward, about Ida, Mitra and Varuna, is ritual material, so leave it out. Wisdomlib's text calls the slope 'Alarm's descent'. I could not check that rendering against the Sanskrit, so do not quote it. Matsyasana is a theme link only, and the Brahmana does not call the fish Vishnu.
found.fit_note: This is the oldest Indian flood story and fits a heavy-rain day almost too well. A small warning is taken seriously, the preparation is done in time, and afterwards you come down slowly. 'As the water subsides, thou mayest gradually descend' is a ready line for 'don't rush back out after the storm', and also for coming out of a backbend or headstand slowly. The fish saves Manu only because Manu first looked after the small fish.
found.translation_used: Julius Eggeling, The Satapatha-Brahmana Part I, Sacred Books of the East vol. 12 (1882)

found.title: King Shibi (Sivi) shelters the frightened pigeon from the hawk
found.source_ref: Mahabharata Book 3 (Vana Parva), Markandeya-Samasya Parva, Section CXCVI in Ganguli. Gutenberg prints the number as 'CLXLVI'; sacred-texts file m03196. An earlier telling with King Usinara, told by the sage Lomasa, is in Vana Parva (Tirtha-yatra Parva) Sections CXXX-CXXXI. In the Sanskrit critical edition (MBh 3.130.19-20 and 3.131), Indra becomes a śyena (hawk) and Agni a kapota (pigeon): 'ūruṃ rājñaḥ samāsādya kapotaḥ śyenajād bhayāt | śaraṇārthī ... bhayapīḍitaḥ', and the king calls it 'kapotasyābhayārthinaḥ' (the pigeon seeking safety, abhaya).
found.story_plain: The gods Agni and Indra decide to test King Sivi. Agni becomes a pigeon and Indra a hawk chasing it. The frightened pigeon falls into the king's lap and asks for protection. The hawk says the pigeon is his food. Sivi answers that whoever hands a frightened creature to its enemy will find no protection when he needs it himself, and he offers a bull and other meat instead. The hawk asks for flesh from the king's own body equal to the pigeon's weight. The pigeon keeps weighing more until Sivi climbs onto the scale himself, without grief. The pigeon then reveals itself as Agni and the hawk as Indra, and Agni promises to make the king's wounds golden and fragrant.
found.key_quote: He that giveth up an affrighted creature seeking protection, unto its foe, doth not obtain protection when he is in need of it himself.
found.safety_notes: The flesh-cutting is graphic: keep it to 'he put himself on the scale' and show no blood. Sivi is a king, so frame the story around protecting the frightened, not around kingship or royalty. Treat Indra and Agni (the testers) with respect. This is not the Vritra story already used. The Shibi version (Section CXCVI) follows the vulgate Ganguli used. In the critical edition the solid version is the Usinara one (3.130-131), so name the king carefully or say 'King Shibi (Ushinara) in some tellings'. In CXCVI the pigeon also claims to be a learned Brahmin sage, which you can leave out.
found.fit_note: When the sky opens and everyone runs for cover, we are all the frightened bird. Shibi is the one who gives shelter instead of locking the door. The pigeon's fear is healthy (it runs to safety), and Shibi does not let fear of loss stop him. The Sanskrit word for the bird, kapota, is exactly the word in Kapotasana, the big Intermediate backbend where students meet their own fear. Ganguli also has Agni promise a son named 'Kapataroman' (pigeon-hair). The Sanskrit says the pigeon came seeking abhaya, the same word the Gita lists first in 16.1 (candidate 5).
found.translation_used: Kisari Mohan Ganguli, The Mahabharata (1883-1896), Project Gutenberg vol. 1. Sanskrit checked on GRETIL (BORI critical edition).

found.title: Bhagavad Gita on fear: a little practice protects (2.40), fearlessness first (16.1), knowing what to fear (18.30)
found.source_ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.40, 16.1, 18.30 and 18.35. Sanskrit: 2.40 'nehābhikrama-nāśo 'sti pratyavāyo na vidyate | svalpam apy asya dharmasya trāyate mahato bhayāt'. 16.1 'abhayaṃ sattva-saṃśuddhir jñāna-yoga-vyavasthitiḥ | dānaṃ damaś ca yajñaś ca svādhyāyas tapa ārjavam'. 18.30 'pravṛttiṃ ca nivṛttiṃ ca kāryākārye bhayābhaye | bandhaṃ mokṣaṃ ca yā vetti buddhiḥ sā pārtha sāttvikī'. Telang cross-check: https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/the-bhagavadgita/d/doc81669.html (ch. 2), doc81683 (ch. 16), doc81685 (ch. 18).
found.story_plain: This is a teaching, not a story. Krishna is teaching the troubled Arjuna about yoga. In 2.40 he says that on this path no effort is wasted, and even a little of it protects from great fear (bhaya). Chapter 16 opens its list of noble qualities with fearlessness (abhayam). In 18.30 he says a clear (sattvic) mind knows what should be feared and what should not. In 18.35 he says that dull (tamasic) steadiness will not give up sleep, fear, sorrow, despondency and folly.
found.key_quote: Arnold, 2.40: "Here shall no end be hindered, no hope marred, / No loss be feared: faith--yea, a little faith-- / Shall save thee from the anguish of thy dread." | 16.1: "Fearlessness, singleness of soul, the will / Always to strive for wisdom" | 18.30: "What should be feared, and what should not be feared". Telang, 2.40: "even a little of this (form of ) piety protects one from great danger". Telang, 18.30: "danger and the absence of danger".
found.safety_notes: The Gita is spoken on a battlefield. Do not show or quote the fighting lines: in Arnold, 2.40 comes right after 'gird thee to the fight'. Keep the war out of frame. Do not overclaim: in 2.40 'dharma' means the yoga of understanding and action, not asana. Arnold renders it 'faith' and Telang 'piety'. Saying '99% practice' or 'practice protects' is the teacher's own application, not the text's meaning. Arnold is a loose verse rendering. For a close line use Telang (SBE vol. 8, 1882). Both are public domain.
found.fit_note: This answers Boonchu's question almost word for word. 18.30 says the wise mind knows what to fear and what not to fear: going home before the flood is wise fear, and panic is not. 2.40 says even a little practice protects from great fear, which suits a short practice on a rainy day. 16.1 puts fearlessness (abhaya) at the top of the list. It pairs well with Shibi's pigeon, which came seeking abhaya.
found.translation_used: Edwin Arnold, The Song Celestial (1885), cross-checked with Kashinath Trimbak Telang, SBE vol. 8 (1882)

found.title: Yoga Sutra 2.9: abhinivesha, the clinging to life that lives even in the wise
found.source_ref: Yoga Sutra 2.9 (Sadhana Pada), with the Yoga-bhashya attributed to Vyasa and Vachaspati Mishra's gloss. Sanskrit: 'svarasavāhī viduṣo 'pi tathārūḍho 'bhiniveśaḥ'. It is the fifth of the five kleshas listed in 2.3.
found.story_plain: This is a teaching, not a story. Patanjali names five afflictions (kleshas), and the last is abhinivesha. Sutra 2.9 says it flows on by its own nature and is present even in the wise. Vyasa's commentary explains it as the craving 'May I not cease to live! May I live!', which he calls the fear of death. He says this fear is found in the very foolish and in the wise alike. Vachaspati Mishra's gloss adds that even a newborn child trembles at the sight of something deadly.
found.key_quote: The will-to-live (abhiniveśa) sweeping on [by the force of] its own nature exists in this form even in the wise. ... In all living beings this craving for one's self ceaselessly rises, 'May I not cease to live! May I live!'
found.asana_link: Savasana / final rest (interpretive link, not in the text)
found.safety_notes: The quote is cleaned from the OCR of the archive.org scan (1966 reprint of Woods' 1914 Harvard Oriental Series translation). The OCR shows 'May I live 1' for 'May I live!' and has typos in one copy of the sutra line. Check against a clean PDF before on-screen text. The commentary goes on to argue for past births. Keep that out unless you want it. Talk of death on a flood day needs a gentle tone with no real victims. The Savasana link is the teacher's own idea and not from the text.
found.fit_note: This explains why even experienced people rush home when the sky turns black: the clinging to life is built into every body, and Patanjali says it is there 'even in the wise'. It is a kind, non-judging way to say that fear is normal and the practice is to see it, not to pretend you have none. It works well as the takeaway after one of the stories.
found.translation_used: James Haughton Woods, The Yoga-System of Patanjali (Harvard Oriental Series 17, 1914), public domain

found.title: The hare who heard a thud: the Daddabha (Duddubha) Jataka
found.source_ref: Jataka No. 322, Daddabha-Jataka (also spelled Duddubha), Cowell ed., The Jataka vol. III (1897), translated by H.T. Francis and R.A. Neil, pp. 49-52 (Pali pp. 74-78).
found.story_plain: A hare lying under a palm sapling at the foot of a vilva tree thinks: if this earth should be destroyed, what would become of me? At that moment a ripe vilva fruit falls on a palm leaf with a thud. He decides the earth is collapsing and runs without looking back. Other hares join him, then deer, boar, buffalo, rhinoceros, tiger, elephant and more, until the running herd is a league long. A young lion (the Bodhisatta) gets in front of them, roars three times and asks who saw the earth breaking. Each animal points to another until they reach the first hare. The lion carries the hare back, finds the fallen fruit, and tells the herd not to be afraid. The text says that without him they would have rushed into the sea and died.
found.key_quote: "I dare not, my lord," said the hare. "Come, don't be afraid," said the lion. ... Alarmed at sound of fallen fruit / A hare once ran away, / The other beasts all followed suit / Moved by that hare's dismay.
found.safety_notes: Leave out the frame story, in which the Buddha calls other ascetics 'heretics' doing 'false asceticism'. That is religious criticism, so do not use it. Do not turn the moral into 'ignore warnings': in Bangkok the flood risk is real. The lesson is to check the actual source, as the lion did. Treat the Bodhisatta-lion with respect. No Ashtanga asana is linked. Simhasana (lion) is not in the Primary or Intermediate sequences.
found.fit_note: This is the 'imagined fear' side of the same rainy day. One thud, or one panicked group-chat message, and a whole forest stampedes. The lion stops, walks back and looks at the real spot. It balances the plover and the three fish: respect real water, but do not join a stampede before you have looked. The question chain ('Who saw it?' 'The elephants know.') makes a funny, fast reel beat.
found.translation_used: E.B. Cowell (ed.), The Jataka vol. III, tr. H.T. Francis and R.A. Neil (Cambridge, 1897), public domain

found.title: BACKUP: The monkey army afraid of the ocean leap, and Jambavan's question to Hanuman
found.source_ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda, Griffith cantos LXV 'The Council', LXVI 'Hanumán' and LXVII 'Hanumán's Speech' (the seed's Kishkindha 65-67).
found.story_plain: The monkey army reaches the ocean and must cross to Lanka, but no one dares the leap, and the army sits in silent despair. Old Jambavan says age has taken his strength, and he will not let young Angad go because the leader must be kept safe. Jambavan turns to Hanuman, who sits silent and apart, and asks him why. He reminds Hanuman that he is the Wind-God's son and that as a child he leapt for the sun. Hanuman rises and grows huge, and the army's fear and sorrow disappear.
found.key_quote: "Why still, and silent, and apart, / O hero of the dauntless heart?" ... Soon as his stature they beheld, / Their fear and sorrow were dispelled;
found.safety_notes: Use this only as a backup, because Hanuman and Surasa have already been used. In Griffith's canto LXVI, Jambavan's account of Hanuman's birth includes the Wind-God's unwanted advance on Anjana. Do not use it. The child Hanuman struck by Indra's thunderbolt is also best left out. The war on Lanka is in the background, so keep it about the leap. The 'forgot his powers because of a sage's curse' version is not in these cantos (it comes from later material), so do not add it. Treat Hanuman as a deity. Hanumanasana is not in the Ashtanga Primary or Intermediate series.
found.fit_note: This is the 'fear stops you' angle: a whole group frozen at the edge of the water, and one elder's reminder of who you are breaks it. Use it only if the other candidates feel too cautious and the reel needs a brave turn. Otherwise prefer the plover and the three fish, which fit the rain better.
found.translation_used: Ralph T.H. Griffith, The Rámáyan of Válmíki (1870-1874), public domain

found.title: Fear and Dread: the Bodhisatta who did not change posture
found.source_ref: Majjhima Nikaya 4, Bhayabherava Sutta (Fear and Dread), segments mn4:20.1 to 20.21 (SuttaCentral numbering). The Buddha is speaking to the brahmin Janussoni at Savatthi. Thanissaro version: https://accesstoinsight.org/tipitaka/mn/mn.004.than.html
found.story_plain: The Buddha tells the brahmin Janussoni what he did before his awakening. On the nights held to be specially portentous (the fourteenth, fifteenth and eighth of the fortnight), he chose to stay in awe-inspiring, hair-raising shrines in parks, forests and trees, hoping to meet fear and dread face to face. While he was there a deer came by, or a peacock snapped a twig, or the wind rustled the leaves, and each time he wondered, 'Is this that fear and dread coming?' Then he asked himself why he kept meditating while expecting fear, and decided to get rid of it as soon as it came, staying just as he was. If fear came while he was walking, he kept walking. If it came while he was standing, sitting or lying down, he stayed standing, sitting or lying down until he had got rid of it.
found.key_quote: "As I was staying there a deer came by, or a peacock snapped a twig, or the wind rustled the leaves. ... Then that fear and dread came upon me as I was walking. I didn't stand still or sit down or lie down until I had got rid of that fear and dread while walking." (Sujato, mn4:20.8, 20.14-20.15). Thanissaro's version of the turning line: "Why do I just keep waiting for fear?"
found.translation_used: Bhikkhu Sujato, Middle Discourses (SuttaCentral, CC0). Checked against Thanissaro Bhikkhu (Access to Insight, 1998, CC BY-NC 4.0).
found.asana_link: No named asana. It fits any held posture: the five breaths in each asana, and the moment in drop-backs or Kapotasana when fear comes and you want to come out. Optional extra: a peacock (mayura) is one of the sounds in the text, and Mayurasana is in the Intermediate Series.
found.safety_notes: Safe. It is a meditation story with no conflict. Make one thing clear: this is about the fear that stays with you after you are safe, not about ignoring real danger. Going home before a flood is still wise, and the reel must not suggest staying out in a storm. Licensing: Sujato's translation is CC0, but the translator 'respectfully requests' that it not be used in AI-derived technologies. Thanissaro's is non-commercial (CC BY-NC), and a studio's Instagram may count as commercial use. The safest option is for Boonchu to say it in his own words and cite 'Majjhima Nikaya 4'.
found.fit_note: Strongest match for today. Every roll of thunder makes the city ask 'is this the flood?', just as the Bodhisatta heard a deer, a twig and the wind and asked 'Is this that fear and dread coming?'. His answer was not to run and not to wait for fear, but to meet it in whatever posture he was in. That is a direct line to holding an asana when fear comes.

found.title: 惊弓之鸟: the wounded goose that fell at the twang of an empty bow
found.tradition: Chinese, Zhan Guo Ce (Strategies of the Warring States)
found.source_ref: Zhan Guo Ce, Chu Ce 4 (楚策四), section 天下合從. The anecdote is told by 魏加 Wei Jia to Lord Chunshen 春申君. The archer is 更羸 Geng Lei (written 更嬴 Geng Ying in some editions). Text checked in the 士禮居叢書本 edition on Wikisource.
found.story_plain: The archer Geng Lei was below a high terrace with the King of Wei when they looked up and saw birds flying. Geng Lei said he could bring a bird down by drawing the bow with no arrow. After a while a wild goose came from the east, and he brought it down with the empty bowstring. Asked how, he said it flew slowly and cried sadly. It flew slowly because an old wound still hurt, and it cried sadly because it had long been separated from its flock. Its old wound had not healed and its fear had not left, so at the sound of the string it strained to fly higher, and because of the old wound it fell.
found.key_quote: 「其飛徐而鳴悲。飛徐者，故瘡痛也；鳴悲者，久失群也，故瘡未息，而驚心未至也。聞弦音，引而高飛，故瘡隕也。」 (Working gloss, not a published translation: 'It flies slowly and cries sadly. Flying slowly: the old wound hurts. Crying sadly: it has long lost its flock. The old wound has not healed and the startled heart has not left. Hearing the string, it pulled up to fly high, and the old wound brought it down.') Bao's edition reads 驚心未去 for 驚心未至.
found.translation_used: Original classical Chinese, 士禮居叢書本 on Wikisource. I found no public-domain English translation. J. I. Crump's 1970 English translation exists but is under copyright and was not checked.
found.asana_link: Dhanurasana / Parsva Dhanurasana (bow pose, Intermediate Series), only because the story turns on a bow that is drawn but never fired
found.safety_notes: Flag. In the source, the anecdote is part of a war-strategy conversation: Wei Jia uses it to argue that Linwu Jun, once beaten by Qin, should not lead the army against Qin. The King of Wei is also there as a bystander. Tell only the archer-and-goose anecdote and leave out the frame. The king can be mentioned in passing but must not become the theme. A bird falls, so keep it gentle. Do not name or show past Bangkok floods with victims. Do not make fun of people who carry flood fear from earlier years.
found.fit_note: Best fit for the word 'again' in the brief. The goose falls not because of an arrow but because of the memory of one. A city that flooded before hears heavy rain the way the goose hears the bowstring. It shows how an old wound turns a harmless sound into a fall. The reel can end on the difference between the real arrow and the twang. The idiom is well known to Chinese audiences, which helps the China cohort.

found.title: The dangerous road: when fear is wisdom (Zhuangzi, Da Sheng)
found.source_ref: Zhuangzi chapter 19, Da Sheng 達生, end of Legge's section 5 (the Tian Kaizhi passage). Zhuangzi puts the words in the mouth of 仲尼 (Confucius). Chinese: 夫畏塗者，十殺一人，則父子兄弟相戒也，必盛卒徒而後敢出焉，不亦知乎！人之所取畏者，袵席之上，飲食之閒，而不知為之戒者，過也！ (Wikisource 莊子/達生)
found.story_plain: This is a short teaching, not a narrative. When a road is known to be dangerous and one traveller in ten is killed on it, families warn each other and will not set out without a large escort, and the text calls this wise. Then it turns: people also face dangers on the mats of their beds and in eating and drinking, but no one warns against those, and the text calls that an error.
found.key_quote: "When people fear the dangers of a path, if one man in ten be killed, then fathers and sons, elder brothers and younger, warn one another that they must not go out on a journey without a large number of retainers;--and is it not a mark of wisdom to do so? But there are dangers which men incur on the mats of their beds, and in eating and drinking; and when no warning is given against them;--is it not a mark of error?" (Legge; a footnote marker and page break in the middle of the passage have been left out)
found.translation_used: James Legge, The Texts of Taoism, Sacred Books of the East vol. 40 (1891), Book XIX. Public domain. Checked against the Chinese on Wikisource and Burton Watson's (copyrighted) version.
found.safety_notes: Mostly safe. 'If one man in ten be killed' refers to danger on the road (Watson says 'murdered'), so keep it general ('a dangerous road') and do not dwell on killing. The same section mentions a man eaten by a tiger, so leave that part out. Present the words as Zhuangzi's text quoting Confucius, without irony toward Confucius.
found.fit_note: This is the clearest classical approval of the user's second theme: fear that keeps you from foolish risk. Rushing home before the flood is the family warning each other about the dangerous road, and the text calls it wise. The twist suits a yoga teacher: we fear the flooded street but not the late nights and the eating and drinking that wear us down. It works well for a 30-second reel.

found.title: The hare who heard the earth breaking (Daddabha Jataka)
found.source_ref: Jataka no. 322, Daddabha-jataka, in The Jataka vol. III, ed. E. B. Cowell, translated by H. T. Francis and R. A. Neil (Cambridge, 1897); Pali page markers [75]-[78] in the online text
found.story_plain: A hare lying under a young palm at the foot of a vilva tree thought, 'If this earth should be destroyed, what would become of me?' At that moment a ripe vilva fruit fell on a palm leaf, and at the sound he fled, sure the earth was collapsing. Other hares joined without looking, then a deer, a boar, an elk, a buffalo, a wild ox, a rhinoceros, a tiger, a lion and an elephant, until the fleeing animals stretched a full league. The Bodhisatta, born as a lion, got ahead of them, roared three times to stop them, and asked who had seen the earth collapsing. Each group pointed to another until it came back to one hare. The lion carried the hare back to the spot, found the fallen fruit on the palm leaf, saw the earth was whole, and told the animals not to be afraid. The text says that without him they would have rushed into the sea and perished.
found.key_quote: "Who saw it collapsing?" ... "They hastened not to view the scene, / But lent a willing ear / To idle gossip, and were clean / Distraught with foolish fear."
found.translation_used: H. T. Francis and R. A. Neil, ed. E. B. Cowell (1897), public domain, on wisdomlib.org
found.safety_notes: Flag the frame story. The Buddha tells this tale about 'heretics' whose austerities he calls false. Leave the frame out so the reel does not mock other religious practices. The opening 'when Brahmadatta reigned in Benares' is only a standard formula and can be dropped. No other issues.
found.fit_note: Very current: on flood days the panic often spreads through LINE groups faster than the water. One sound, then a chain of 'someone said', then a stampede. The lion's single question, 'Who saw it?', is a simple message: check the real forecast before you run. It also pairs well with the Zhuangzi road passage, since checking is not the same as dismissing.

found.title: 杞人忧天: the man of Qi who feared the sky would fall
found.source_ref: Liezi chapter 1, Tian Rui 天瑞, the passage beginning 杞國有人憂天地崩墜 (Giles places it in his chapter I, 'Cosmogony'). Chinese text checked at https://zh.wikisource.org/zh-hant/%E5%88%97%E5%AD%90/%E5%A4%A9%E7%91%9E%E7%AF%87
found.story_plain: A man of the state of Qi was so afraid that heaven and earth would collapse, leaving him nowhere to be, that he could neither sleep nor eat. Someone who pitied him explained that the sky is only accumulated air we breathe and move in all day, and the earth is only accumulated matter we walk on all day. Both men were relieved and happy. Then Changluzi laughed at them both: rainbows, clouds, mist, wind and rain make up the heavens, and heaven and earth must one day pass away, though to fear that they will fall now is far from the truth. Master Liezi heard this and smiled: saying they will be destroyed is wrong, and saying they will not be destroyed is also wrong. Whether they are destroyed or not, why should he trouble his mind about it?
found.key_quote: "There was once a man in the Ch'i State who was so afraid the universe would collapse and fall to pieces, leaving his body without a lodgment, that he could neither sleep nor eat." / "Rainbows, clouds and mist, wind and rain, the four seasons--these are perfected forms of accumulated ether, and go to make up the heavens." / "Whether destruction awaits the world or no, why should I trouble my head about it?"
found.translation_used: Lionel Giles, Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh-Tzu (1912), public domain
found.safety_notes: Safe, with one important framing point. Today's flood risk is real, so the reel must not suggest that people who rush home are like the man of Qi. Draw the line between the reasonable step (go home) and the worry that stops you from eating and sleeping. Note that Giles inserts his own explanatory paragraph into the middle of Changluzi's speech, so do not quote that part as Liezi.
found.fit_note: Liezi's ending has more depth than the familiar idiom. Even the 'wise' man who mocks the worrier is told he is only half right, and the sky he describes is made of 'wind and rain', today's weather. The question it leaves is not 'will it fall?' but 'how much of my mind will I give to it?'. It is a familiar chengyu for the China audience. It overlaps with the hare and the snake-in-the-cup stories, so choose one of the three.

found.title: 杯弓蛇影: the snake in the wine cup
found.source_ref: Earliest version: Ying Shao 應劭, Fengsu Tongyi 風俗通義, chapter Guai Shen 怪神 (Wikisource 風俗通義/9), in the entry headed 世間多有見怪驚怖以自傷者 ('In the world many people see strange things, are terrified, and harm themselves'). Later version: Jin Shu 晉書 juan 43, biography of Yue Guang 樂廣 (https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E6%99%89%E6%9B%B8/%E5%8D%B7043).
found.story_plain: Ying Shao tells this about his own grandfather, Ying Chen, magistrate of Ji. On the summer solstice Chen invited his registrar Du Xuan to drink. A red crossbow hanging on the north wall was reflected in the cup and looked like a snake. Du Xuan was afraid but did not dare refuse. He drank, and that same day got sharp pains in his chest and belly that no treatment could cure. When Chen visited and learned that Du Xuan believed a snake had got into his belly, he thought for a long time, noticed the hanging crossbow, and had Du Xuan brought back to the same place and served wine. The 'snake' appeared again, Chen told him it was only the crossbow's shadow on the wall, Du Xuan's mind cleared, and he recovered. The Jin Shu tells the same kind of story about Yue Guang and a guest, where the reflection came from a horn on the wall painted as a snake.
found.key_quote: Fengsu Tongyi: 「此壁上弩影耳，非有他怪。」 (Working gloss: 'This is only the shadow of the crossbow on the wall; there is nothing strange.') Jin Shu: 「酒中復有所見不？」答曰：「所見如初。」廣乃告其所以，客豁然意解，沈屙頓愈。
found.translation_used: Original classical Chinese on Wikisource. I found no public-domain English translation; the English glosses here are working glosses only.
found.safety_notes: Safe. One accuracy point: the idiom says 弓 (bow), but the Fengsu Tongyi has a crossbow (弩) and the Jin Shu has a horn (角) painted as a snake, so do not say 'a bow' as if it came from the source text. The illness is caused by fear and is cured, and no one dies. I could not fully read the Fengsu Tongyi text myself because of Wikisource rate limits; the summary and the quoted line were confirmed through two separate fetch and search results.
found.fit_note: The cure is the strong teaching moment: the healer does not say 'don't be afraid'. He brings the man back to the same seat, the same cup and the same 'snake', and shows him where it comes from. For a teacher that maps onto returning to the posture you fear and looking at it in good light. It makes a good quick Reel with the chengyu on screen for the China audience. It overlaps with the Liezi and hare stories.

found.title: The swimmer in the Lüliang falls
found.source_ref: Zhuangzi chapter 19, Da Sheng 達生, Legge section 9. Chinese: 孔子觀於呂梁，縣水三十仞，流沫四十里，黿鼉魚鼈之所不能游也 ... 與齊俱入，與汩偕出，從水之道而不為私焉。此吾所以蹈之也。(Wikisource 莊子/達生)
found.story_plain: Confucius was looking at the waterfall at Lüliang, where the water fell thirty ren (Legge: 240 cubits) and the spray ran forty li, water where no turtle, alligator or fish could swim. He saw a man swimming in it and, thinking he was suffering and meant to die, sent his disciples along the bank to pull him out. A few hundred paces on, the man came out and walked along the bank singing, his hair loose. Confucius asked whether he had a special way of treading water. The man said he had none: he went in with the swirl, came out with the eddy, and followed the way of the water without setting himself against it. He had been born among those hills and grew up by that water, so it had become his nature.
found.key_quote: "I enter and go down with the water in the very centre of its whirl, and come up again with it when it whirls the other way. I follow the way of the water, and do nothing contrary to it of myself;--this is how I tread it."
found.translation_used: James Legge, The Texts of Taoism, SBE vol. 40 (1891), Book XIX, public domain. Burton Watson's (copyrighted) line for comparison: 'I go under with the swirls and come out with the eddies, following along the way the water goes and never thinking about myself.'
found.asana_link: Kurmasana (tortoise, Primary Series), Nakrasana (crocodile, Intermediate Series) and Matsyasana (fish, finishing sequence). They are named after the kinds of creature the text says could not swim in that water (黿鼉魚鼈, which Legge gives as tortoise, gavial, fish, turtle).
found.safety_notes: Flag twice. (1) The text says Confucius thought the man was suffering and wanted to die, which is a suicide reference, so leave that line out of the reel. (2) On a flood day, a hero who plunges into raging water is the wrong message. The reel must not suggest people go into floodwater, and must stress that he was raised in that water from birth. Low suitability for today, so hold it for a different reel.
found.fit_note: It shows both sides of fear. What looks deadly to the watchers is home to someone who has trained in it all his life. Confucius's alarm is reasonable for someone who has not trained, and the swimmer's calm is earned, not reckless. It fits a message about daily practice turning fear into familiarity. The three asana names give a playful hook. Because of the flood context it is better used on a dry day.

verdicts.corrected_story_plain: The Buddha tells the brahmin Janussoni, at Jeta's Grove near Savatthi, what he did before his awakening. On the nights held to be specially portentous (the fourteenth, fifteenth and eighth of the fortnight), he chose to stay in awe-inspiring, hair-raising shrines in parks, forests and trees, hoping he might see that fear and dread. While he was there a deer came by, or a peacock snapped a twig, or the wind rustled the leaves, and each time he wondered, 'Is this that fear and dread coming?' Then he asked himself why he always meditated expecting the fear to come, and decided to get rid of it just as it came, staying just as he was. If fear came while he was walking, he kept walking. If it came while he was standing, sitting or lying down, he stayed standing, sitting or lying down until he had got rid of it.
verdicts.corrected_quote: "As I was staying there a deer came by, or a peacock snapped a twig, or the wind rustled the leaves. Then I thought, ‘Is this that fear and dread coming?’ Then I thought, ‘Why do I always meditate expecting that fear to come? Why don’t I get rid of that fear and dread just as it comes, while remaining just as I am?’ Then that fear and dread came upon me as I was walking. I didn’t stand still or sit down or lie down until I had got rid of that fear and dread while walking." (Sujato, mn4:20.8-20.15). Thanissaro's turning line, exactly as printed: "Why do I just keep waiting for fear?"
verdicts.quote_translator: Bhikkhu Sujato (Middle Discourses, SuttaCentral, CC0). Second line: Thanissaro Bhikkhu (Access to Insight, 1998, CC BY-NC 4.0).
verdicts.corrected_source_ref: Majjhima Nikaya 4, Bhayabherava Sutta (Fear and Dread), mn4:3.1 ("Before my awakening") and mn4:20.1-20.21 (SuttaCentral segment numbers). Setting: Jeta's Grove, Anathapindika's monastery, near Savatthi (mn4:1.2); the listener is the brahmin Janussoni (mn4:2.1).
verdicts.problems: No factual errors. Every story detail matches Sujato mn4:20.1-20.21 and the Thanissaro version. The candidate's key quote is word for word, with two lines left out at the ellipsis; the corrected quote restores them. The Thanissaro line "Why do I just keep waiting for fear?" is exact. The two translators differ in small ways: Thanissaro has "a wild animal" where Sujato has "a deer" (Pali mago), and "fear & terror" where Sujato has "fear and dread". The licence claims are confirmed. Sujato's MN entry reads: "dedicated to the public domain via Creative Commons Zero (CC0)... The translator respectfully requests that any use be in accordance with the values and principles of the Buddhist community. In particular, please do not use this work in AI training datasets, for the development of any AI model or algorithm, or in any AI-derived technologies." Thanissaro's page is CC BY-NC 4.0.
verdicts.asana_claim_note: The link is a theme, not a named asana. Holding a posture through fear matches the text's 'remaining just as I am'. The optional peacock link holds up: the Pali is moro (Sanskrit mayura), and Mayurasana is in the Ashtanga Intermediate Series. Kapotasana and drop-backs as fear points are teaching commentary, not from the text.
verdicts.safety_notes: Safe: it is a meditation story with no conflict, no victims and no mockery. Keep the candidate's framing: the story is about fear that comes when nothing is actually happening, not about ignoring a real flood warning. Going home before the flood stays the wise choice. Licensing: Sujato's request against AI-derived use also covers an AI-drafted script, and Thanissaro's text is non-commercial only. The safest option is for Boonchu to tell it in his own words and cite 'Majjhima Nikaya 4'.

verdicts.corrected_story_plain: The archer Geng Lei was standing with the King of Wei below the Jing terrace (an old note reads jing as 'high') when they looked up and saw birds flying. Geng Lei said he could bring a bird down just by drawing the bow and releasing it with no arrow. After a while a wild goose came from the east, and he brought it down with the empty bowstring. He told the king it was a bird that had already been wounded. Asked how he knew, he said it flew slowly and cried sadly. It flew slowly because an old wound still hurt, and it cried sadly because it had long been separated from its flock. The old wound had not healed and its fright had not left it (this follows Bao Biao's reading; the Shiliju base text has a harder reading here). When it heard the sound of the string it pulled up to fly high, and the old wound brought it down.
verdicts.corrected_quote: 「其飛徐而鳴悲。飛徐者，故瘡痛也；鳴悲者，久失群也，故瘡未息，而驚心未至也。聞弦音，引而高飛，故瘡隕也。」 (Shiliju edition, as printed. Bao Biao's edition reads 去 for 至: 驚心未去.)
verdicts.quote_translator: No translator. This is the classical Chinese original. Any English is a working gloss only, not a published translation.
verdicts.corrected_source_ref: Zhan Guo Ce 戰國策, juan 17, Chu Ce 4 (楚四), section 天下合從. Zhao sends 魏加 Wei Jia to Lord Chunshen 春申君 of Chu. Wei Jia tells the story of the archer 更羸 Geng Lei and the King of Wei at the 京臺. Text from the 士禮居叢書本 on Wikisource, with notes from Bao Biao (鮑本) and the 札記.
verdicts.source_url_checked: https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=%E6%88%B0%E5%9C%8B%E7%AD%96_(%E5%A3%AB%E7%A6%AE%E5%B1%85%E5%8F%A2%E6%9B%B8%E6%9C%AC)/%E6%A5%9A/%E5%9B%9B&action=raw (raw wikitext of the same page; the rendered candidate URL returned HTTP 429)
verdicts.problems: 1) The Chinese key quote matches the Shiliju text character for character, and the note that Bao reads 去 for 至 is correct. However, the candidate's English gloss 'the startled heart has not left' translates Bao's 去, not the 至 printed in the quoted Chinese. The 札記 says the current text (今本) reads 去, and another note gives 未忘 ('not forgotten'). Label the gloss as following Bao's reading. 2) The text adds a small detail: before explaining, Geng Lei tells the king 「此孽也」, 'this one is a wounded/stricken one'. 3) 京臺 may be a terrace name rather than simply 'a high terrace'; Bao glosses 京 as 'high' and another note says it may be the terrace's name. 4) The frame is confirmed: Wei Jia, sent by Zhao, uses the story to argue that Linwu Jun, 'once a stricken bird of Qin' (嘗為秦孽), should not be made the general against Qin, during the vertical alliance (合從) against Qin. 5) The alternate spelling 更嬴 and the Crump 1970 translation were not checked; this edition has only 更羸.
verdicts.asana_claim_note: Dhanurasana and Parsva Dhanurasana really are in the Ashtanga Intermediate Series, and the link is honestly labelled as theme only (a bow drawn with no arrow). It is a loose link. Krounchasana (heron) in the same series is another bird-themed option, but it is equally only a theme.
verdicts.safety_notes: Usable only without the frame. In the source, the anecdote serves a military-strategy argument about choosing a general against Qin during an anti-Qin alliance. Leave out the frame, Lord Chunshen, Linwu Jun and Qin. The King of Wei is only a bystander and can be named in passing, but must not become the theme. A bird falls, so keep it gentle. Do not show or name past Bangkok floods with victims, and do not make fun of people who carry flood memories from earlier years.

verdicts.corrected_story_plain: This is a short teaching, not a narrative. When a road is known to be dangerous and one traveller in ten is killed on it, fathers and sons and brothers warn each other and will not set out without a large escort, and the text calls this wise. Then it turns: the dangers people should really fear are on the mats of their beds and in eating and drinking, yet no one warns against those, and the text calls that an error.
verdicts.corrected_quote: "When people fear the dangers of a path, if one man in ten be killed, then fathers and sons, elder brothers and younger, warn one another that they must not go out on a journey without a large number of retainers;--and is it not a mark of wisdom to do so? But there are dangers which men incur on the mats of their beds, and in eating and drinking; and when no warning is given against them;--is it not a mark of error?" (Legge; a footnote marker after 'error' and a page break {p. 18} are left out)
verdicts.quote_translator: James Legge, The Texts of Taoism, Sacred Books of the East vol. 40 (1891), Book XIX. Public domain.
verdicts.corrected_source_ref: Zhuangzi ch. 19 Da Sheng 達生. It is the 仲尼曰 paragraph right after the Tian Kaizhi 田開之 and Duke Wei of Zhou 周威公 dialogue, at the end of Legge's section 5 (Legge pp. 17-18). Chinese (Wikisource 莊子/達生): 夫畏塗者，十殺一人，則父子兄弟相戒也，必盛卒徒而後敢出焉，不亦知乎！人之所取畏者，袵席之上，飲食之閒，而不知為之戒者，過也！
verdicts.problems: The Legge quote is word for word, and the Chinese matches Wikisource exactly. The comparison 'Watson says murdered' is confirmed: "if they hear that one traveler in a party of ten has been murdered". Two cautions. (1) Who is speaking depends on the translator. Legge and the Wikisource punctuation put the whole passage inside Confucius's (Kung-ni's) speech. Watson closes the Confucius quote after 'stand stock-still in the middle' and gives the dangerous-road lines without a clear speaker. The safest wording is 'the Zhuangzi says'. (2) The fit note reads 'the mats of their beds' as 'late nights'; that is our interpretation, not the text. Watson has 'lying in bed or sitting around eating and drinking'. A secondary search result says Wang Fuzhi reads 袵席之上 as bedroom (sexual) indulgence; I did not open that commentary, so this is not confirmed. Say 'the bed and the table', not 'late nights', when quoting.
verdicts.asana_claim_note: No asana link is claimed, which is correct; none exists in the text.
verdicts.safety_notes: Safe if it stays general. Say 'a dangerous road' and do not dwell on killing. Leave out the man eaten by a tiger and the man who died of fever; both are in the Tian Kaizhi speech just before this passage. Present the words neutrally ('the Zhuangzi says'), without irony toward Confucius. Do not suggest 'bed' matters in a sexual sense. This passage supports the decision to go home before the flood.

verdicts.corrected_story_plain: A hare lying under a young palm at the foot of a vilva tree thought, 'If this earth should be destroyed, what would become of me?' At that moment a ripe vilva fruit fell on a palm leaf. At the sound he thought the solid earth was collapsing and fled without looking back. Another hare saw him running and followed, then another, until a hundred thousand hares were fleeing. A deer, a boar, an elk, a buffalo, a wild ox, a rhinoceros, a tiger, a lion and an elephant heard that the earth was breaking up and fled too, until the fleeing animals stretched a full league. The Bodhisatta, born as a lion, got ahead of them at the foot of a mountain, roared three times to stop them, and asked who had seen the earth collapsing. Each group pointed to another until it came back to one hare. The lion carried the hare on his back to the spot, found the ripe fruit on the palm leaf, saw the earth had not broken up, came back and told the animals not to be afraid. The text says that without him they would all have rushed into the sea and perished.
verdicts.corrected_quote: "Who saw it collapsing?" ... "They hastened not to view the scene, / But lent a willing ear / To idle gossip, and were clean / Distraught with foolish fear."
verdicts.quote_translator: H. T. Francis and R. A. Neil, The Jataka vol. III, ed. E. B. Cowell (Cambridge University Press, 1897). Public domain. (Wisdomlib's series header credits 'Robert Chalmers, 1895', but that is the label for the whole six-volume set; volume III is by Francis and Neil.)
verdicts.corrected_source_ref: Jataka no. 322, Daddabha-jataka, The Jataka vol. III, ed. E. B. Cowell, tr. H. T. Francis and R. A. Neil (1897). Pali page markers [75]-[78] on wisdomlib.
verdicts.problems: Small fix. The candidate says 'Other hares joined without looking', but the text says the FIRST hare fled 'without so much as looking behind him'. The other hares saw him running and joined the chase 'till one hundred thousand hares all took to flight together', a detail the candidate left out. (The later verse does say 'They hastened not to view the scene'.) All other details check out: the list of animals and its order, 'a full league', the lion getting ahead 'to the foot of a mountain' and roaring three times, the chain of 'we don't know, the X know', the hare carried on the lion's back, and 'all the beasts would have rushed into the sea and perished'. 'Who saw it collapsing?' and the verse are word for word. The page markers [75]-[78] are correct.
verdicts.asana_claim_note: No asana link is claimed, which is correct.
verdicts.safety_notes: Leave out the frame story. In it, the Buddha uses the tale to dismiss 'heretics' who 'made their beds on thorns' and practised 'false asceticism' near Jetavana, which would mock other religious practices. The 'when Brahmadatta reigned in Benares' opening is only a formula and can be dropped. Another framing point the candidate missed: the hare panics at rumour, but today's rain is real. The reel must not compare people heeding real weather or flood warnings to the hares. The lesson is to check before spreading or believing rumours (LINE-group panic), not to ignore warnings.

verdicts.corrected_story_plain: A man of the small state of Qi (杞, not the larger state 齊) was so afraid that heaven and earth would collapse, leaving him nowhere to be, that he could neither sleep nor eat. Someone who worried about his worry went to explain: the sky is only piled-up air, and we bend, stretch and breathe in it all day; the sun, moon and stars are only bright things in that air and could not hurt us even if they fell; the earth is only piled-up matter, and we walk on it all day. Both men were relieved and happy. Then Changluzi heard about it and laughed: rainbows, clouds, mist, wind and rain and the four seasons make up the heavens, and mountains, rivers, metals and rocks make up the earth, so who can say they will never be destroyed? To fear that they will fall now is far from the truth, but to say they will never be destroyed is also not right. Master Liezi heard this and smiled: saying they will be destroyed is wrong, and saying they will not be destroyed is also wrong. Whether they are destroyed or not, why should he let it trouble his mind?
verdicts.corrected_quote: "There was once a man in the Ch'i State who was so afraid the universe would collapse and fall to pieces, leaving his body without a lodgment, that he could neither sleep nor eat." / "Rainbows, clouds and mist, wind and rain, the four seasons--these are perfected forms of accumulated ether, and go to make up the heavens." / "Whether destruction awaits the world or no, why should I trouble my head about it?"
verdicts.quote_translator: Lionel Giles, Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh-Tzu (1912), Book I 'Cosmogony'. Public domain.
verdicts.corrected_source_ref: Liezi ch. 1 Tian Rui 天瑞, the passage beginning 杞國有人憂天地崩墜，身亡所寄，廢寢食者 and ending 壞與不壞，吾何容心哉. Giles, Book I 'Cosmogony'.
verdicts.problems: No errors in the story details. All three Giles quotes are word for word, and the Chinese matches Wikisource. Points to know. (1) 'Qi' here is 杞 (Qǐ), easily confused with 齊 (Qí). Giles's 'Ch'i' covers both, so put the character on screen. (2) The helper's 'air we breathe and move in all day' follows the Chinese (若屈伸呼吸，終日在天中行止) more closely than Giles. Giles has 'Processes of contraction and expansion, inspiration and expiration are continually taking place up in the heavens', so do not quote the paraphrase as Giles. (3) Changluzi himself already says both sides fall short (憂其壞者，誠爲大遠；言其不壞者，亦爲未是), then ends with 'when the time comes, why would one not worry?' Liezi says both claims are 'wrong' (亦謬). So the fit note's 'only half right' is loose; Liezi sets the whole debate aside. (4) Confirmed: Giles puts his own explanatory paragraph ('The speaker means that...') just before the last sentence of Changluzi's speech ('Who, having to face the day of disruption, would not be alarmed?'). Do not quote that paragraph as Liezi.
verdicts.asana_claim_note: No asana link is claimed, which is correct.
verdicts.safety_notes: Safe: no conflict, victims or mockery of religion. Keep the candidate's framing: the reel must not suggest that people who rush home before a real flood are like the man of Qi. The contrast is between a sensible step (go home) and worry that stops you from eating and sleeping. Changluzi's 'laughing' should not become mockery of the worrier in the reel.

verdicts.corrected_story_plain: Confucius was looking at the waterfall at Lüliang, where the water fell thirty ren (Legge: 240 cubits) and the spray ran forty li, water in which no turtle, alligator or fish could swim. He saw a man swimming in it and, thinking he was in some trouble, sent his disciples along the bank to pull him out. A few hundred paces on, the man came out and walked along the bank singing, his hair loose. Confucius followed him and said he had first taken him for a ghost, then asked whether he had a special way of treading water. The man said he had none: he went in with the swirl, came out with the eddy, and followed the way of the water without setting himself against it. He had been born among those hills and was at home there; he grew up by that water and was at home in it, so it had become his nature.
verdicts.corrected_quote: "I enter and go down with the water in the very centre of its whirl, and come up again with it when it whirls the other way. I follow the way of the water, and do nothing contrary to it of myself;--this is how I tread it."
verdicts.quote_translator: James Legge, The Texts of Taoism, Sacred Books of the East vol. 40 (1891), Book XIX. Public domain. Watson comparison, confirmed as printed: "I go under with the swirls and come out with the eddies, following along the way the water goes and never thinking about myself."
verdicts.corrected_source_ref: Zhuangzi ch. 19 Da Sheng 達生, Legge section 9 (pp. 20-21). Chinese (Wikisource 莊子/達生): 孔子觀於呂梁，縣水三十仞，流沫四十里，黿鼉魚鼈之所不能游也。見一丈夫游之 ... 與齊俱入，與汩偕出，從水之道而不為私焉。此吾所以蹈之也。
verdicts.problems: No errors. The Legge quote is word for word, the Chinese matches Wikisource, and Watson's comparison line is exact. Minor points: Legge calls the swimmer 'an old man', but the Chinese 丈夫 just means 'a grown man', so 'a man' is fine. Legge's animals are 'tortoise, gavial, fish, or turtle', and his verb is 'play', not 'swim'. Legge renders the place as 'the cataract near the gorge of Lü'. In the corrected story I softened 'meant to die' to 'in some trouble' for safety. The text actually says 以為有苦而欲死也, 'thought he was suffering and wanted to die'.
verdicts.asana_claim_note: All three poses are where the candidate says: Kurmasana in the Primary Series, Nakrasana in the Intermediate Series, Matsyasana in the finishing sequence. The match with 黿鼉魚鼈 (giant softshell turtle, Chinese alligator, fish, softshell turtle) is loose but fair: kurma = tortoise, nakra = crocodile, matsya = fish. It is correctly labelled theme only.
verdicts.safety_notes: Not suitable for today's flood reel. (1) The source line says Confucius thought the man was suffering and wanted to end his life, a suicide reference, so leave it out or soften it. (2) On a day of flood fear, a hero who plunges into raging water sends the wrong message; it could be read as encouraging people to enter floodwater. If used later on a dry day, stress that he was born and raised in that water, and add nothing that invites viewers to copy him. Confucius's alarm should be shown as reasonable, not mocked.

found.title: Seneca: we suffer more in imagination than in reality
found.source_ref: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius (Epistulae Morales), Letter 13 'On Groundless Fears', sections 4-5 (key line 13.4); also 13.8, 13.10, 13.12-13
found.story_plain: Seneca writes a letter to his younger friend Lucilius. He says a fighter only gains real confidence after being knocked down and getting up again. Then he says there are more things likely to frighten us than to crush us, and we suffer more in imagination than in reality. He sorts our worries into three kinds: things that hurt us more than they should, before they should, or when they should not hurt at all. He advises checking whether the proof of a coming trouble is sure, instead of believing rumour. He allows prudence, but tells Lucilius to weigh his hopes as well as his fears.
found.key_quote: There are more things, Lucilius, likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
found.safety_notes: Safe if you stay with sections 4-5, 10, 12-13. Avoid 13.8 (soldiers fleeing camp, and rumour 'which is wont to settle wars'), 13.11 (executioners, sword at the throat) and 13.14 (Socrates' hemlock, Cato's sword, which is a suicide). Do not bring in Seneca's life at Nero's court; that is government and politics. The asana link is only a teaching parallel (students fear the drop-back long before anything happens). No text links Seneca to any asana.
found.fit_note: Today people rush home picturing the flood before a drop has fallen. Seneca names that exactly: 'not to be unhappy before the crisis comes' (13.4), and 'some torment us before they ought' (13.5). He is not reckless either. 13.8 says 'consider whether your proofs of future trouble are sure' and warns against 'that mocker, rumour', which suits flood rumours on LINE and social media. 13.12 adds 'let prudence help you'. So the reel can say: check the real forecast and leave early if it says so, but don't live the flood in your head all afternoon. Other exact lines: 13.10 'what does it avail to run out to meet your suffering? You will suffer soon enough, when it arrives'; 13.13 'we are frightened at uncertainties, just as if they were certain.'
found.translation_used: Richard Mott Gummere, Loeb Classical Library, Ad Lucilium Epistulae Morales vol. 1 (1917), as transcribed on Wikisource

found.title: Montaigne: the disease of fear
found.source_ref: Montaigne, Essays, Book III, Chapter 13 'Of Experience' (the last essay), passage on living with his kidney stone
found.story_plain: In his last essay, 'Of Experience', Montaigne writes about living with kidney stones. He says he still moves about as before and rides after his hounds. When he feels something stirring, he does not keep checking his pulse or his urine to look for trouble. He says he will feel the pain soon enough, without making it more and longer by 'the disease of fear.' He adds that he judges himself by actual sensation, not by reasoning about what may come.
found.key_quote: I shall soon enough feel the pain, without making it more and longer by the disease of fear. He who fears he shall suffer, already suffers what he fears.
found.safety_notes: The context is his own chronic illness (kidney stones). The passage just before mentions blood from his kidneys, so leave out the medical detail and just say 'an illness'. No victims, no politics. Do NOT use his other essay Book I ch. 17 'Of Fear' ('The thing in the world I am most afraid of is fear'): its examples are battles, sieges and a murder. Translator note: the Gutenberg text is Charles Cotton's translation as revised and edited by William Carew Hazlitt (1877), not raw Cotton. Florio's wording was not checked.
found.fit_note: This is the short, quotable line for the end of the reel. You can use it on its own or put it next to Seneca. 'He who fears he shall suffer, already suffers what he fears' fits people who already feel flooded while the sky is only grey. It also has a 'fear stops you' side: in spite of his illness Montaigne still 'ride[s] after my hounds' as before.
found.translation_used: Charles Cotton, edited by William Carew Hazlitt (Project Gutenberg eBook #3600)

found.title: Odysseus tied to the mast
found.source_ref: Homer, Odyssey, Book XII (Circe's advice, then passing the Sirens)
found.story_plain: On the way home by sea, the goddess Circe warns Ulysses (Odysseus) about the Sirens, whose singing keeps sailors from ever coming home. She tells him to stop his men's ears with wax, and if he wants to hear the song himself, to have them bind him standing upright to the mast. If he begs to be freed, they must bind him tighter. He tells the crew everything, so that 'whether we live or die we may do so with our eyes open.' As they pass, he hears the song and frowns at his men to free him, but Eurylochus and Perimedes bind him tighter until they are out of hearing. Then the men take the wax from their ears and untie him.
found.key_quote: Therefore pass these Sirens by, and stop your men’s ears with wax that none of them may hear; but if you like you can listen yourself, for you may get the men to bind you as you stand upright on a cross piece half way up the mast, and they must lash the rope’s ends to the mast itself, that you may have the pleasure of listening. If you beg and pray the men to unloose you, then they must bind you faster.
found.safety_notes: Butler calls him 'Ulysses' throughout, and the key quote drops a footnote marker '99' after 'mast'. Circe's speech has a gruesome line ('a great heap of dead men’s bones lying all around, with the flesh still rotting off them'): leave it out. The Sirens' song mentions the Trojan War only in passing, which is fine as far background. Stop the story at the Sirens: Scylla, who comes next, eats six of his men. The Gutenberg text has a typo, 'I look a large wheel of wax' (should be 'took'): don't quote that line. The asana link is thematic only: 'baddha' means bound, and staying still in a bind while the mind wants to move. No text connects them.
found.fit_note: This is wise fear rather than panic. Odysseus does not deny the danger. He knows his own weakness and sets things up beforehand (wax, ropes, a rule that 'if I beg, bind me tighter'). That is what sensible rain prep looks like: decide in advance when you will leave and what you will do, so panic in the moment can't change the plan. 'With our eyes open' is a strong spoken line.
found.translation_used: Samuel Butler, The Odyssey (1900), Project Gutenberg eBook #1727

found.title: Daedalus and Icarus: fly the middle way
found.source_ref: Ovid, Metamorphoses Book 8, Daedalus and Icarus (More's section markers [183]-[235]; the advice is at [200])
found.story_plain: Daedalus wants to escape Crete. Sea and land are blocked, so he says the sky is the way out. He makes wings of feathers bound with thread and wax, while his son Icarus plays with the feathers and the wax. Before they fly he warns Icarus to keep the middle way: too low and the waters will weigh the wings down, too high and the sun will scorch them. As they fly past the islands, Icarus, 'proud of his success,' leaves his father and climbs toward the sky. The sun softens the wax, the feathers come away, and he falls into the sea, which is now named after him. His father finds the wings floating on the waves.
found.key_quote: My son, I caution you to keep the middle way, for if your pinions dip too low the waters may impede your flight; and if they soar too high the sun may scorch them. Fly midway.
found.safety_notes: A child dies by falling into the sea. In a week of flood fear, drowning images are sensitive, so tell the death in one line or end at the warning. The escape is from Minos, a king. Keep him off-screen and don't make royalty a theme. The Minotaur and Theseus passage just before is unrelated and violent, so skip it. Brookes More's translation is from 1922, so it's in the US public domain. The Bakasana (Intermediate Series) link is only a teaching parallel: lean too far forward and you tip, too little and you drop.
found.fit_note: This is the most balanced story on the list. The father warns against BOTH extremes: too high (reckless) and too low (the water drags you down). So it isn't 'fear is good' or 'fear is bad'. It is the middle way, like rain day: don't ignore the storm, but don't let panic run your day. Water is even one of the two dangers in the warning.
found.translation_used: Brookes More, Ovid's Metamorphoses (1922), as hosted on theoi.com

found.title: The Two Frogs and the Well
found.source_ref: Aesop, 'The Two Frogs' (the frogs and the well), in Townsend's Three Hundred Aesop's Fables (1867)
found.story_plain: Two frogs live in the same pool. In the summer heat the pool dries up, so they set out together to find another home. On the way they pass a deep well full of water. One frog says they should go down and live there, since it will give them shelter and food. The other answers with more caution: what if the water fails us, how would we get out again from such a depth? The fable ends with its moral: do nothing without a regard to the consequences.
found.key_quote: “But suppose the water should fail us. How can we get out again from so great a depth?”
found.safety_notes: There is no death and no politics in this one. Townsend does not say what the frogs decide, so don't add an ending. The asana link is checked: Bhekasana (frog pose) is in the Ashtanga Intermediate Series, and Sanskrit bheka means 'a frog'. The dictionaries on wisdomlib also give bheka as '2) A timid man. 3) A cloud' (Apte), and Monier-Williams has 'a cloud' and 'a timid man (= bhīru)'. Apte and Shabda-Sagara derive it from bhī, 'to fear' (Uṇādi-sūtra 3.43), but Monier-Williams says 'probably onomatopoetic'. So say 'traditional grammarians link the word to fear', not 'it means fear'. Dictionary source: https://www.wisdomlib.org/definition/bheka
found.fit_note: This is the safest and closest fit for today: water, the wish to rush to the first shelter you see, and one calm frog who thinks about how to get back out. The asana gives a hook too: the frog pose's Sanskrit name, bheka, can also mean 'a timid man' and 'a cloud', so the frog pose holds both the rain cloud and the timid one. A second wording in V. S. Vernon Jones's 1912 translation, 'The Frogs and the Well' (Gutenberg #11339), reads: 'Not so fast, my friend: supposing this well dried up like the marsh, how should we get out again?' with the moral 'Think twice before you act.'
found.translation_used: George Fyler Townsend, Three Hundred Aesop's Fables (1867), Project Gutenberg eBook #21

found.title: The Ant and the Grasshopper
found.source_ref: Aesop, 'The Ant and the Grasshopper' (Perry Index 373), in Joseph Jacobs, The Fables of Aesop (Macmillan, 1894)
found.story_plain: One summer's day a grasshopper hops about in a field, chirping and singing. An ant passes by, working hard to carry an ear of corn to the nest. The grasshopper asks the ant to stop and chat instead. The ant says it is laying up food for the winter and tells the grasshopper to do the same. The grasshopper asks why bother about winter when there is plenty of food now. When winter comes, the grasshopper has no food and is dying of hunger, while it watches the ants share out grain from their stores.
found.key_quote: It is best to prepare for the days of necessity.
found.safety_notes: The big risk with this one: in a flood week, the moral can sound like 'people who got flooded didn't prepare and deserved it'. Never aim it at people hurt by real floods. Keep it to 'prepare yourself'. In Townsend and Vernon Jones the ants mock the grasshopper ('dance supperless to bed'; 'they chuckled'), so don't copy the mockery. The asana link has a caveat. Salabhasana (Ashtanga Intermediate Series) comes from Sanskrit śalabha, 'a grass-hopper, locust' (Monier-Williams; Apte also gives 'a moth'). But Aesop's Greek original is a cicada (tettix), and 'grasshopper' comes from later English translations. So it matches the English story, not the Greek. Dictionary source: https://www.wisdomlib.org/definition/shalabha
found.fit_note: This is foresight: prepare before the hard season so you don't have to panic when it comes. The V. S. Vernon Jones translation (1912, Gutenberg #11339, 'The Grasshopper and the Ants') even has rain in it: 'One fine day in winter some Ants were busy drying their store of corn, which had got rather damp during a long spell of rain.' Locust pose gives a direct visual. Townsend (1867) opens: 'THE ANTS were spending a fine winter’s day drying grain collected in the summertime.'
found.translation_used: Joseph Jacobs, The Fables of Aesop (1894), Project Gutenberg eBook #28

found.title: The Fox and the Lion
found.source_ref: Aesop, 'The Fox and the Lion', in Townsend's Three Hundred Aesop's Fables (1867); also Jacobs, The Fables of Aesop (1894)
found.story_plain: A fox who has never seen a lion meets one by chance in the forest and is so frightened he nearly dies of fear. The second time they meet, he is still very alarmed, but less than before. By the third time he has grown so bold that he walks up to the lion and starts a friendly conversation. Townsend's moral: acquaintance softens prejudices.
found.key_quote: WHEN A FOX who had never yet seen a Lion, fell in with him by chance for the first time in the forest, he was so frightened that he nearly died with fear. On meeting him for the second time, he was still much alarmed, but not to the same extent as at first. On seeing him the third time, he so increased in boldness that he went up to him and commenced a familiar conversation with him.
found.safety_notes: There is no violence and no death. Use Townsend. Jacobs calls the lion 'the King of Beasts', which is a small royalty touch to avoid. No Ashtanga asana is named after a fox or a lion in Primary or Intermediate, so the Kapotasana link is only a teaching parallel: a pose many students are scared of the first time, less the second, and familiar by the third. Don't present it as a textual link.
found.fit_note: This adds a fear type the others miss: fear shrinks when you keep meeting it. Bangkok has been through many heavy rains, and the first storm feels worse than the tenth. It cuts both ways, which gives the reel a turn. Jacobs's moral for the same fable is 'Familiarity breeds contempt.' Get used to the rain, but don't stop respecting it. Jacobs's wording: 'The third time they came near one another the Fox went straight up to the Lion and passed the time of day with him'.
found.translation_used: George Fyler Townsend, Three Hundred Aesop's Fables (1867), Project Gutenberg eBook #21

found.title: The Hares and the Frogs (FLAG: do not use as main story)
found.source_ref: Aesop, 'The Hares and the Frogs', in Townsend's Three Hundred Aesop's Fables (1867); also Jacobs, The Fables of Aesop (1894)
found.story_plain: The hares are tired of always being afraid. Together they decide to end their lives by jumping from a high cliff into a deep lake. As they run toward the lake, the frogs on the bank hear their feet and rush into the deep water to hide. One hare sees this and calls to the others to stop. He tells them there are creatures even more timid than they are.
found.key_quote: “Stay, my friends, do not do as you intended; for you now see that there are creatures who are still more timid than ourselves.”
found.safety_notes: FLAG, DROP AS MAIN STORY. In every version checked, the hares set out to kill themselves by drowning: Townsend says 'put an end to themselves', Jacobs 'determined to drown themselves', Vernon Jones 'intending to drown themselves'. Suicide plus drowning in a flood week is too sensitive for a public reel. You can't tell it honestly without that detail, and dropping it would change the story. Use The Two Frogs and the Well instead for the frog / Bhekasana link.
found.fit_note: It holds up as a text and fits the theme. In Jacobs the hares panic and run when 'they saw a troop of wild Horses stampeding about', much like people rushing home in the rain, and Jacobs's moral is 'There is always someone worse off than yourself.' But the suicide intent rules it out (see safety notes). It is listed only because it was one of the seeds to check.

verdicts.corrected_story_plain: Seneca writes to his younger friend Lucilius. He says a prizefighter can only go into a fight with real confidence if he has been knocked down before and got up again. Then he says there are more things likely to frighten us than to crush us, and we suffer more often in imagination than in reality. His advice is not to be unhappy before the crisis comes, because the danger may never arrive. He sorts our worries into three kinds: some torment us more than they ought, some before they ought, and some when they ought not to torment us at all. When someone says 'something will happen', he says first check whether your proofs of future trouble are sure, and don't let rumour make a fool of you. If we let our fears run as far as they can, he says, there is no end to our sorrows. So let prudence help you, temper fear with hope, and weigh your hopes as well as your fears.
verdicts.corrected_quote: There are more things, Lucilius, likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
verdicts.quote_translator: Richard Mott Gummere (Loeb Classical Library, Ad Lucilium Epistulae Morales vol. 1, 1917), as transcribed on Wikisource
verdicts.corrected_source_ref: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius (Epistulae Morales), Letter 13 'On Groundless Fears', section 4 (key line); also sections 2, 5, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13
verdicts.problems: No factual errors. I checked every quote word for word against the Wikisource Gummere text: 13.4 key line; 13.4 'not to be unhappy before the crisis comes'; 13.5 'some torment us before they ought'; 13.8 'First of all, consider whether your proofs of future trouble are sure' and 'we are mocked by that mocker, rumour'; 13.10 'what does it avail to run out to meet your suffering? You will suffer soon enough, when it arrives'; 13.12 'let prudence help you'; 13.13 'we are frightened at uncertainties, just as if they were certain.' All of them match. Two nuances. (1) In 13.12, prudence is called in AGAINST over-fearing. The full line is 'if we indulge our fears to the greatest possible extent; in this matter, let prudence help you, and contemn with a resolute spirit even when it is in plain sight.' So 'he allows prudence' slightly spins it. 'Check the real forecast and leave early if it says so' is the teacher's own application of 13.8 ('check your proofs'), not Seneca's words, and should be presented that way. (2) The candidate's safety note says to avoid 13.8, but its fit note quotes 13.8. That is fine if you use only the 'proofs' sentence and 'that mocker, rumour'. Cut 'which is wont to settle wars' and the soldiers fleeing camp. An extra exact line worth using is 13.9: 'That is why no fear is so ruinous and so uncontrollable as panic fear. For other fears are groundless, but this fear is witless.'
verdicts.asana_claim_note: Theme only, and honestly labeled. No text links Seneca to any asana. Urdhva Dhanurasana and drop-backs work as a teaching parallel (fear of the drop-back before anything happens). Never present it as a textual link.
verdicts.safety_notes: Safe if you use 13.4-5, 13.8 (first sentence plus 'mocker, rumour' only), 13.9, 13.10, 13.12-13. Cut these: 13.2's violent fight detail ('seen his own blood', 'teeth rattle beneath his opponent's fist'), so just say 'knocked down and got up again'; 13.8 'wont to settle wars' and the soldiers abandoning camp; 13.11 sword at the victim's throat and executioners; 13.14 Socrates' hemlock and Cato's sword (a suicide); 13.17 'political career'. Leave out Seneca's life at Nero's court. Don't let the 'imagined fear' message come across as 'ignore flood warnings'. Pair it with 13.8: check the real evidence.

He says he still moves about as before and rides after his hounds. If he feels something stirring, he does not trouble himself to check his pulse or his urine and start some annoying precaution. He will feel the pain soon enough, he says, without making it more and longer by the disease of fear. He judges himself only by actual sensation, not by reasoning, and brings nothing to it but expectation and patience.
verdicts.corrected_quote: I shall soon enough feel the pain, without making it more and longer by the disease of fear. He who fears he shall suffer, already suffers what he fears.
verdicts.quote_translator: Charles Cotton, edited by William Carew Hazlitt (1877), Project Gutenberg eBook #3600
verdicts.corrected_source_ref: Montaigne, Essays, Book III, Chapter XIII 'Of Experience' (the final essay), passage on living with the stone
verdicts.problems: None factual. The quote is word for word in the Gutenberg text. 'ride after my hounds', 'consult my pulse or my urine' and 'I only judge of myself by actual sensation, not by reasoning' are all confirmed. The Gutenberg header lists translator Charles Cotton and editor William Carew Hazlitt, and the edition is dated 1877 (preface signed 'KENSINGTON, November 1877'). Caution: the sentences right after the quote attack doctors' 'false prognostics'. Don't stretch that into 'forecasts are useless'. Montaigne is talking about medicine, and that message would contradict sensible flood preparation.
