The surrounding text has 'the least motion forces pure blood out of my kidneys', 'wastes and consumes the substance of my kidneys and my life', and just after the quote 'Old age excepted, which is an indubitable sign of the approach of death'. No politics, no victims. Agree: don't use Book I ch. 17 'Of Fear' (battles, sieges).

verdicts.corrected_story_plain: On the way home by sea, the goddess Circe warns Ulysses (Odysseus) about the Sirens. Anyone who sails too close and hears their song never comes home to his wife and children. She tells him to stop his men's ears with wax. If he wants to hear the song himself, the men must bind him standing upright on a crosspiece half way up the mast, and if he begs to be freed, they must bind him faster. Before they reach the Sirens' island he tells his men Circe's warning about the Sirens. He says it is not right that only one or two of them should know, so 'that whether we live or die we may do so with our eyes open.' He gives the order himself: if he begs to be set free, bind him more tightly. He kneads wax soft and stops his men's ears, and they bind him to the mast. When the Sirens sing, he longs to hear more and frowns at his men to free him. They row harder, and Eurylochus and Perimedes bind him with stronger bonds until they are out of hearing. Then the men take the wax from their ears and untie him.
verdicts.corrected_quote: Therefore pass these Sirens by, and stop your men’s ears with wax that none of them may hear; but if you like you can listen yourself, for you may get the men to bind you as you stand upright on a cross piece half way up the mast, and they must lash the rope’s ends to the mast itself, that you may have the pleasure of listening. If you beg and pray the men to unloose you, then they must bind you faster.
verdicts.quote_translator: Samuel Butler, The Odyssey (1900), Project Gutenberg eBook #1727 (footnote marker 99 after 'mast' omitted)
verdicts.corrected_source_ref: Homer, Odyssey, Book XII: Circe's advice about the Sirens, then Ulysses' speech to his crew and the passing of the Sirens' island
verdicts.problems: Error fixed: 'He tells the crew everything' is wrong. His speech promises to share Circe's prophecies but covers only the Sirens. A few lines later Butler has him say outright: 'I said nothing about the awful monster Scylla, for I knew the men would not go on rowing if I did, but would huddle together in the hold.' So don't present 'eyes open' as telling them the whole truth. Everything else is confirmed word for word: the key quote (Butler prints footnote marker 99 after 'mast'), 'whether we live or die we may do so with our eyes open', 'made signs by frowning to my men that they should set me free', 'Eurylochus and Perimedes bound me with still stronger bonds', 'my men took the wax from their ears and unbound me', the typo 'I look a large wheel of wax', the gruesome bones line, and the Sirens' song mentioning 'the Argives and Trojans before Troy'. A shorter spoken line in Ulysses' own words: 'If I beg and pray you to set me free, then bind me more tightly still.' Butler's translation date of 1900 is confirmed in the Gutenberg front matter.
verdicts.asana_claim_note: Theme only, and honestly labeled. Monier-Williams (via wisdomlib.org/definition/baddha) gives baddha as 'bound, tied, fixed, fastened, chained, fettered' and also 'stopped, checked, restrained', so the 'bound' parallel with Baddha Padmasana is linguistically sound. No text connects Odysseus to the pose.
verdicts.safety_notes: Safe if you stop at the Sirens. Cut 'warble him to death with the sweetness of their song' and 'a great heap of dead men’s bones lying all around, with the flesh still rotting off them'. Scylla comes next and 'snatched up my six best men' and 'munch[ed] them up', so don't go on. The Trojan War is only far background in the Sirens' song, which is acceptable. He cuts the wax with his sword, which is trivial. Don't quote the typo line.

verdicts.corrected_story_plain: Daedalus wants to escape Crete. Sea and land are blocked, so he says the sky is the way out. He makes wings of feathers, binding the middle ones with thread and fixing the lower ones with wax, while his son Icarus plays with the feathers and softens the wax with his thumb. Before they fly he warns Icarus to keep the middle way: too low and the waters may hold back his flight, too high and the sun may scorch his wings. As they fly past the islands, Icarus, 'proud of his success', leaves his father and climbs toward the sky. The sun melts the wax, the feathers are gone, and he falls into the sea, which is now named after him. His father finds the wings floating on the waves.
verdicts.corrected_quote: My son, I caution you to keep the middle way, for if your pinions dip too low the waters may impede your flight; and if they soar too high the sun may scorch them. Fly midway.
verdicts.quote_translator: Brookes More, Ovid's Metamorphoses (Boston: Cornhill Publishing, 1922), as hosted on theoi.com
verdicts.corrected_source_ref: Ovid, Metamorphoses Book 8, 'Daedalus and Icarus' (theoi.com markers [183] to before [236]; the warning is in the [200] block, the fall in the [220] block)
verdicts.problems: No errors. The quote is word for word in More (theoi; the line breaks fall differently in the verse). Confirmed: the theoi page states 'TRANSLATED BY BROOKES MORE'. The page shows no date, but bibliographic sources give Cornhill Publishing, Boston, 1922. I confirmed 'Proud of his success, the foolish Icarus forsook his guide', 'now called Icarian', and 'he saw the wings of his dear Icarus, floating on the waves'. Small wording note: More says the waters may 'impede your flight', not 'weigh the wings down', so I adjusted the paraphrase to match. The passage ends at [235]; [236] starts the Perdix story.
verdicts.asana_claim_note: Theme only. Bakasana is in the Ashtanga Intermediate Series (Bakasana A and B). The balance parallel (lean too far and you tip, too little and you drop) is a teaching image, not a textual link.
verdicts.safety_notes: A child drowns, which is sensitive in a flood week. Tell the fall in one line or end at the warning. Leave out 'He found the body on an island shore ... to bury the unfortunate remains' and 'the dead boy's name'. Keep Minos off-screen and don't quote 'though Minos may be lord of all the world his sceptre is not regnant of the air' (it makes a king the theme). Do not continue into [236]+: there Daedalus, 'enraged and envious, sought to slay' his nephew Perdix by casting him from a temple. Skip the Minotaur and Theseus material before [183].

verdicts.corrected_story_plain: Two frogs live in the same pool. In the summer heat the pool dries up, so they set out together to find another home. On the way they pass a deep well full of water. One frog says they should go down and live there, since it will give them shelter and food. The other answers more cautiously: what if the water fails us? How would we get out again from such a depth? The fable ends with its moral: do nothing without a regard to the consequences.
verdicts.corrected_quote: “But suppose the water should fail us. How can we get out again from so great a depth?”
verdicts.quote_translator: George Fyler Townsend, Three Hundred Aesop's Fables (1867), Project Gutenberg eBook #21
verdicts.corrected_source_ref: Aesop, 'The Two Frogs' (the frogs and the well; the FIRST of two fables with this title in Townsend), Three Hundred Aesop's Fables (1867); compare V. S. Vernon Jones, 'The Frogs and the Well' (1912)
verdicts.problems: No errors. The Townsend story, the quote and the moral are word for word. The Vernon Jones alternative is also exact: 'Not so fast, my friend: supposing this well dried up like the marsh, how should we get out again?' with the moral 'Think twice before you act.' Watch out: Townsend has a SECOND, different fable also titled 'The Two Frogs' (one frog in a pond, one in a gully by a road). That frog refuses to move and 'a heavy wagon ... crushed him to death'. Don't confuse or merge the two. I checked the dictionary claims on wisdomlib and they are exact. Apte: '[bhī kan kasya netvam; Uṇādi-sūtra 3.43] 1) A frog ... 2) A timid man. 3) A cloud'. Shabda-Sagara: '1. A frog. 2. A cloud. 3. A timid man ... E. bhī to fear'. Monier-Williams: '(probably onomatopoetic; but cf. Uṇādi-sūtra iii, 43) a frog ... a cloud ... a timid man (= bhīru)', with the cloud and timid-man senses marked as from lexicographers. The Pali Text Society dictionary also says 'onomat.', while a Pali-Myanmar dictionary on the same page gives a traditional gloss 'sappato bhāyatīti bheko' ('it fears the snake, so it is bheka'). The candidate's wording 'traditional grammarians link the word to fear, not it means fear' is correct.
verdicts.asana_claim_note: Confirmed as same figure. Bhekasana (frog pose) is in the Ashtanga Intermediate Series, after Salabhasana A/B, and bheka means 'a frog'. Treat the extra 'timid man' and 'cloud' senses as dictionary (lexicographers') meanings. Say 'Sanskrit dictionaries also list', not that the pose name means fear.
verdicts.safety_notes: Clean: no death, no politics, no mockery. Townsend gives no ending, so don't invent one. Make sure the reel uses the well fable, not Townsend's other 'The Two Frogs' (frog crushed by a wagon).

verdicts.corrected_story_plain: One summer's day a grasshopper hops about in a field, chirping and singing. An ant passes by, working hard to carry an ear of corn to the nest. The grasshopper asks the ant to come and chat instead of toiling. The ant says it is helping to lay up food for the winter and advises the grasshopper to do the same. The grasshopper asks why bother about winter when there is plenty of food now. When winter comes, the grasshopper has no food and finds itself dying of hunger, while it sees the ants handing out corn and grain every day from the stores they collected in the summer. Moral: it is best to prepare for the days of necessity.
verdicts.corrected_quote: It is best to prepare for the days of necessity.
verdicts.quote_translator: Joseph Jacobs, The Fables of Aesop (London: Macmillan, 1894), Project Gutenberg eBook #28
verdicts.corrected_source_ref: Aesop, 'The Ant and the Grasshopper' (Perry Index 373), in Joseph Jacobs, The Fables of Aesop (Macmillan, 1894)
verdicts.problems: No errors. The Jacobs story and moral are word for word (title page: Macmillan, 1894). Perry 373 and the Greek original being a cicada are confirmed on Wikipedia ('in the original, a cicada'). I did not check the Greek word tettix in a Greek text myself. Townsend's opening, 'THE ANTS were spending a fine winter’s day drying grain collected in the summertime.', and 'dance supperless to bed' are exact. Vernon Jones's rain line, 'One fine day in winter some Ants were busy drying their store of corn, which had got rather damp during a long spell of rain.', and 'they chuckled' are exact. Extra find from the same wisdomlib page: Monier-Williams lists śālabha (with vidhi) as 'the way of the moth (to fly into fire i.e. “rushing inconsiderately into danger”)' [Mudrārākṣasa]. That is a dictionary-attested idiom tying the śalabha word to reckless risk, useful for the 'fear protects you' side. Cite it as a dictionary idiom only, because the Mudrārākṣasa is a political court drama.
verdicts.asana_claim_note: Valid with the caveat. Salabhasana is in the Ashtanga Intermediate Series. On wisdomlib, Monier-Williams gives śalabha as 'a grass-hopper, locust ... a kind of moth' and Apte gives '1) A grass-hopper, locust ... 2) A moth'. The 'same figure' match holds for the English grasshopper, not the Greek cicada. Say that openly or keep it as a visual echo.
verdicts.safety_notes: Main risk: in a flood week the moral can sound like 'people who got flooded didn't prepare'. Aim it only at your own preparation, never at people hurt by real floods. Don't copy the ants' mockery ('dance supperless to bed', 'they chuckled'). Jacobs's grasshopper 'found itself dying of hunger'. Keep that light or leave it out.

verdicts.corrected_story_plain: A fox who has never seen a lion meets one by chance in the forest and is so frightened he nearly dies of fear. The second time they meet, he is still very alarmed, but less than before. The third time he has grown so bold that he walks up to the lion and starts a friendly conversation. Townsend's moral: acquaintance softens prejudices.
verdicts.corrected_quote: WHEN A FOX who had never yet seen a Lion, fell in with him by chance for the first time in the forest, he was so frightened that he nearly died with fear. On meeting him for the second time, he was still much alarmed, but not to the same extent as at first. On seeing him the third time, he so increased in boldness that he went up to him and commenced a familiar conversation with him.
verdicts.quote_translator: George Fyler Townsend, Three Hundred Aesop's Fables (1867), Project Gutenberg eBook #21
verdicts.corrected_source_ref: Aesop, 'The Fox and the Lion' (the FIRST of two fables with this title in Townsend: the three meetings), Three Hundred Aesop's Fables (1867); also Jacobs, The Fables of Aesop (1894)
verdicts.problems: No errors. The Townsend quote and the moral 'Acquaintance softens prejudices.' are word for word. The Jacobs wording is confirmed: 'The third time they came near one another the Fox went straight up to the Lion and passed the time of day with him', plus the moral 'Familiarity breeds contempt.' Jacobs does call the lion 'the King of Beasts'. Watch out: Townsend has a second, different fable also titled 'The Fox and the Lion' (a fox reviles a caged lion). Don't mix them up.
verdicts.asana_claim_note: Theme only, and honestly labeled. No Primary or Intermediate pose is named after a fox or a lion. Kapotasana (Intermediate Series) as a 'scary first time, familiar by the third' pose is a teaching parallel only.
verdicts.safety_notes: Clean: no violence, no death. Use Townsend to avoid Jacobs's 'King of Beasts'. If you use Jacobs's 'Familiarity breeds contempt', make the turn clear: get used to the rain but keep respecting it. Don't let it read as 'stop taking floods seriously'.

verdicts.corrected_story_plain: The hares are weary of their own great timidity and of always being afraid. Together they decide to put an end to themselves by jumping from a high cliff into a deep lake. As they run toward the lake, the frogs on the bank hear their feet and rush into the deep water for safety. One hare sees this and calls to the others to stop, because there are creatures even more timid than they are.
verdicts.corrected_quote: “Stay, my friends, do not do as you intended; for you now see that there are creatures who are still more timid than ourselves.”
verdicts.quote_translator: George Fyler Townsend, Three Hundred Aesop's Fables (1867), Project Gutenberg eBook #21
verdicts.corrected_source_ref: Aesop, 'The Hares and the Frogs', Townsend, Three Hundred Aesop's Fables (1867); also Jacobs (1894) and Vernon Jones (1912)
verdicts.problems: The text checks out: Townsend's quote is word for word, as are 'put an end to themselves and their troubles by jumping from a lofty precipice into a deep lake below', Jacobs's 'troop of wild Horses stampeding about', 'determined to drown themselves', and 'There is always someone worse off than yourself.', and Vernon Jones's 'intending to drown themselves'. Vernon Jones also adds 'killed and devoured them daily'. The verdict is about textual accuracy only. The story is unusable for safety reasons (see safety_notes).
verdicts.asana_claim_note: The frogs are only a side detail. The hares are the main figures, so 'same figure' with Bhekasana is weak. In any case the story is dropped. Use The Two Frogs and the Well for the Bhekasana link.
verdicts.safety_notes: DROP. In every translation checked (Townsend, Jacobs, Vernon Jones), the core plot is a group suicide by drowning. In a flood week that is too sensitive for a public reel, and leaving the detail out would falsify the story. Do not use it, even as a secondary example.

asanas.name: Tittibhasana
asanas.series: Intermediate (Nadi Shodhana): Tittibhasana A, B and C after Yoganidrasana. Some lists also have a D. It also appears as a passing position in Primary: on the way out of Bhujapidasana (Tittibhasana, then Bakasana) and on the way into Kurmasana (vinyasa 7), according to the ashtangayoga.info vinyasa charts.
asanas.sanskrit_word_meaning: Monier-Williams p.429 col.3 spells the word ṭiṭṭibha, with retroflex ṭ. There is no 'tittibha' entry with dental t. The entry reads: 'ṭiṭṭibha m. = ˚bhaka (also ṭīṭibha, q.v.), Gaut.; Mn. v, 11; Yājñ. i, 172; MBh. xii &c. | N. of a Daitya | of a Dānava (enemy of Indra in the 13th Manv-antara), GarP. | of a bug, Kathās. lx, 128 | n. a kind of leprosy, Gal. | ṭiṭṭibhī f. the female of the Ṭiṭṭibha bird, R. (G) ii, 8, 43.' The next entry: 'ṭiṭṭibhaka m. the bird Parra jacana, L.' So the main meaning is a bird. The only insect sense is 'of a bug', meaning the personal name of a bug character in Kathāsaritsāgara ch. 60. The PW dictionary agrees ('N. pr. ... einer Wanze', the name of a bedbug), and Tawney's 1880 translation calls him 'a flea, named Tiṭṭibha'. MW never gives 'firefly'. The MW words for firefly are kha-jyotis ('a shining flying insect, fire-fly') and kha-dyota. Other dictionaries: Apte has 'A kind of bird' and quotes Pt. 1.314. Benfey has 'A bird, Parra jacuna, or goensis'. Shabda-Sagara has 'A bird (Parra jacana or goensis.) E. ṭiṭṭi imitative sound', so the bird is named after its call. 'Lapwing' comes from a Kannada dictionary (cited on wisdomlib). 'Sand-piper (Tringa goensis)' comes from a note quoting Bate and Śabdasāgara (wisdomlib, Jain glossary). The bird is very likely the red-wattled lapwing: Wikipedia lists 'Lobivanellus goensis' as a synonym, and that bird's Kannada name is still tittibha. Wikipedia's 'small insect, firefly' cites Yoga Journal 2007, not a dictionary.
asanas.story_link_honest_wording: SAY: 'Tittibhasana is named after the ṭiṭṭibha, a small shore bird (a lapwing or plover), not a firefly. The same bird is the hero of a Panchatantra fable about fear.' CHECKED STORY (Panchatantra Book I; Ryder 1925, 'The Plover Who Fought the Ocean'): the hen is about to lay her eggs and says, 'Here is the ocean near at hand. His tide might some day make a long reach and lick away my babies.' The cock refuses to move. She tells him the turtle story and the three-fish story. The ocean takes the eggs. The birds go to Garuda, Vishnu orders the ocean, and it gives the eggs back. The Sanskrit (GRETIL, Jha ed.) says the ocean returned them 'sa-bhayena', meaning 'in fear'. FEAR LINE: Panc. 1.343 in the Jha edition (Apte numbers it Pt. 1.314) reads 'utkṣipya ṭiṭṭibhaḥ pādāv āste bhaṅga-bhayād divaḥ'. Literally: 'the ṭiṭṭibha lies with its feet raised, out of fear (bhaya) that the sky will break.' Ryder's version: 'The plover lies with claws upstretched / To prop the falling sky.' Hindi has a matching folk saying: 'Will the sky be supported by the sand-piper?' Of the eight asanas, this is the only one where the asana's word and the word for fear appear together in a classical line. DON'T SAY the pose was named after this fable or this proverb. No Ashtanga source documents that. Wikipedia reports that ashtangayoga.info tells the bird-and-ocean story as a symbol for the pose; I could not open that page. Comparing 'legs up off the floor' in the pose with the bird's raised feet is our own observation, so present it that way. LEAVE OUT: the hen saying she will burn herself (self-harm), and the frame story (a jackal pushing a bull to fight a lion king).

asanas.name: Kurmasana
asanas.series: Primary (Yoga Chikitsa): Kurmasana, then Supta Kurmasana, right after Bhujapidasana.
asanas.sanskrit_word_meaning: MW p.300 col.2: 'kūrma m. a tortoise, turtle, VS.; TS. &c.' Other senses: 'the earth considered as a tortoise swimming on the waters'; 'a particular figure or intertwining of the fingers (mudrā), Tantras.'; 'one of the outer winds of the body (causing the closing of the eyes), Vedāntas.'; 'N. of a deity'; 'of a serpent or Kādraveya king'; 'of a Ṛṣi (son of Gṛtsa-mada)'; 'Viṣṇu's second incarnation (descent in the form of a tortoise to support the mountain Mandara at the churning of the ocean)'.
asanas.story_link_honest_wording: SAY: 'Kurmasana means tortoise posture. The same word, kūrma, is used for...' Two checked uses. (1) Panchatantra Book I, the story the frightened ṭiṭṭibha hen tells her mate. Ryder calls it 'Shell-Neck, Slim, and Grim'; Tawney names the tortoise Kambugrīva, with two swans. In a drought, two birds carry the turtle through the air on a stick held in his mouth. He promises silence, speaks when people below chatter, and falls. The Sanskrit sums it up as 'sa kūrma iva durbuddhiḥ kāṣṭhād bhraṣṭo' ('like the foolish tortoise fallen from the stick'). Ryder's moral: 'To take advice from kindly friends / Be ever satisfied'. The point is good caution: don't open your mouth in the middle of a risk. (2) Bhagavad Gita 2.58: the tortoise drawing in its limbs stands for drawing in the senses. Arnold 1885: 'As the wise tortoise draws its four feet safe / Under its shield, his five frail senses back / Under the spirit's buckler from the world / Which else assails them'. This frames pulling back as wisdom, not cowardice, which fits rushing home before the flood. DON'T SAY the pose is named after the Kurma avatar or after either story. FLAGS: the Gita is spoken on a battlefield, so use only the tortoise image and not the setting. In the Panchatantra the turtle is 'cut to bits' by townspeople; just say he fell.

asanas.name: Matsyasana
asanas.series: Finishing sequence, practised after every series: after Sarvangasana, Halasana, Karnapidasana, Urdhva Padmasana and Pindasana, and followed by Uttana Padasana. Not to be confused with Ardha Matsyendrasana (Intermediate), which uses Matsyendra, 'lord of fishes'.
asanas.sanskrit_word_meaning: MW p.776 col.3: 'matsya m. (cf. matsa and maccha) a fish, RV. &c. &c. (personified as a prince with the patr. Sāmmada, ŚBr.)'. Other senses: 'a partic. species of f˚'; '(du.) the 12th sign of the zodiac (Pisces)'; '(pl.) N. of a people and country'; 'N. of Virāṭa'.
asanas.story_link_honest_wording: SAY: 'Matsyasana means fish posture. Matsya is the same word as the fish that warned Manu of the flood.' CHECKED: Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.8.1, where the Sanskrit is 'matsyaḥ pāṇī ā pede' ('a fish came into his hands'). Eggeling 1882 (SBE 12): 'Rear me, I will save thee!' 'Wherefrom wilt thou save me?' 'A flood will carry away all these creatures: from that I will save thee!' ... 'In such and such a year that flood will come. Thou shalt then attend to me (i.e. to my advice) by preparing a ship.' Fear turns into preparation, which fits a rain and flood reel exactly. SECOND CHECKED USE: the three fish ('trayo matsyāḥ') in Panchatantra Book I, again told by the ṭiṭṭibha hen. Anāgata-vidhātā ('Forethought') hears fishermen and leaves early. Pratyutpanna-mati ('Readywit') plays dead. Yad-bhaviṣya ('Fatalist', 'whatever will be') stays and is caught. Moral (Ryder): 'Forethought and Readywit thrive; / Fatalist can't keep alive.' DON'T SAY the pose honours Vishnu's Matsya avatar. In the ŚB the fish is not called Vishnu (that identification is later, Puranic), and I found no Ashtanga source naming the pose after the avatar. FLAGS: keep the myth flood clearly apart from real Bangkok flooding and any real victims. Fatalist is clubbed, so just say he was caught.
asanas.sources: MW: https://www.sanskrit-lexicon.uni-koeln.de/scans/csl-apidev/getword.php?dict=mw&key=matsya&input=slp1&output=iast. Eggeling, Satapatha Brahmana Part 1 (SBE 12), archive.org item wg912, 1.8.1.1-6. Sanskrit 'matsyaḥ' confirmed at https://sanskritreadingroom.wordpress.com/2018/06/04/satapatha-brahma%E1%B9%87a-a-fish-saves-manu-from-the-flood/. Three fish: Ryder https://shreevatsa.net/ryder/old/dfnp/2009-restart/ryder.html; GRETIL 'anāgatavidhātādi-matsya-traya-kathā'; Tawney 'Story of the three Fish' https://www.gutenberg.org/files/40588/40588-h/40588-h.htm. Series: https://www.ashtangayoga.info/asana-vinyasa/pdf/Vinyasa-Finishing.pdf

asanas.name: Kapotasana
asanas.series: Intermediate: Kapotasana A and B, after Laghu Vajrasana and before Supta Vajrasana. Related poses: Raja Kapotasana and Eka Pada Raja Kapotasana are in Advanced A, and Eka Pada Kapotasana is in Advanced B (grimmly syllabus lists).
asanas.sanskrit_word_meaning: MW p.251 col.2: 'kapota m. (√kav ...; fr. 2. ka + pota?), a dove, pigeon, (esp.) the spotty-necked pigeon (in the Vedas often a bird of evil omen), RV.; AV.; VS.; MBh. &c.' Other senses: 'a bird in general, L.'; 'a frieze, cornice'; 'a particular position of the hands'; 'the grey colour of a pigeon'; 'the grey ore of antimony'. Also 'kapotī f. the female of a pigeon, Pañcat.'
asanas.story_link_honest_wording: SAY: 'Kapota means dove or pigeon. It is the same word as the doves in the Panchatantra net story.' CHECKED: Panchatantra Book II. A hunter's net traps a whole flock of doves. Their leader Citragrīva (Ryder calls him 'Gay-Neck') says to them 'na bhetavyam', 'do not be afraid' (Sanskrit 'kapotān ūce ... na bhetavyam'). Ryder: 'Have no fear, my friends. For / Provided judgment does not fail, / Whatever the distress, / Men reach the farther shore of woe'. They all fly up at once and carry the net away ('proceeded without fear'). The point is to meet fear with a clear head and do it together. ALSO CHECKED: Rig Veda 10.165 is a hymn to make a frightening dove harmless. Griffith: 'Gods, whatsoe'er the Dove came hither seeking, sent to us as the envoy of Destruction' and 'Auspicious be the Dove that hath been sent us, a harmless bird'. This matches MW's 'bird of evil omen'. DON'T SAY the pose was named after either text. FLAGS: the leader is a 'dove-king' (an animal fable, low risk). Ryder's nearby verses mention Ravan stealing a wife and Yudhishthira's gambling; leave those out. RV 10.165 ends by paying reverence 'to Death, to Yama', which is heavy, so use it lightly. Avoid the King Shibi dove-and-hawk story (royalty theme).

asanas.name: Bakasana
asanas.series: Intermediate: Bakasana A and B, after Supta Vajrasana. It is also a passing position in Primary, on the way out of Bhujapidasana (ashtangayoga.info chart).
asanas.sanskrit_word_meaning: MW p.719 col.1: 'baka m. (also written vaka) a kind of heron or crane, Ardea Nivea (often fig. = a hypocrite, cheat, rogue, the crane being regarded as a bird of great cunning and deceit as well as circumspection), Mn.; MBh. &c.' Other senses: Sesbana grandiflora; an apparatus for calcining metals; N. of Kubera; of a demon; 'of an Asura (said to have assumed the form of a crane and to have been conquered by Kṛṣṇa), BhP.'; 'of a Rākṣasa killed by Bhīma-sena, MBh.'; 'of a Ṛṣi (Dālbhya)'. Also 'bakī f. a female crane'.
asanas.story_link_honest_wording: SAY: 'Baka means crane or heron, the same word as the crane in the Panchatantra story about fear used as bait.' CHECKED: Panchatantra Book I, 'baka-kulīraka-kathā' (Ryder: 'The Heron That Liked Crab-Meat'). An old heron frightens the pond. In Ryder's version he says fishermen are coming. In the Jha Sanskrit text he says astrologers predict a 12-year drought. He offers to fly the fish to a safe lake and eats them on a rock. The crab sees the heap of bones. Before he acts, the crab recites (Ryder): 'Fear fearful things, while yet / No fearful thing appears; / When danger must be met, / Strike, and forget your fears.' Two lessons: ask who profits from your fear, and fear early, then act calmly. MW's own 'circumspection' fits this too. I did NOT find this verse at this point in the Jha Sanskrit edition, so credit it to Ryder's translation. A similar Sanskrit maxim, 'tāvad bhayasya bhetavyaṃ yāvad bhayam anāgatam', is reported in the Hitopadesha (search result, not opened). DON'T SAY the pose is named after this story. FLAGS: the crab cuts off the heron's head, so soften it. Avoid the Bakāsura stories (killed by Bhīma or Krishna; violence).

asanas.name: Bhairavasana
asanas.series: Advanced A (Third series, Sthira Bhaga): Vasishthasana, Vishvamitrasana, Kashyapasana, Chakorasana, then Bhairavasana, then Skandasana and Durvasasana. In this pose the foot goes behind the head while the body is held in a side plank.
asanas.sanskrit_word_meaning: MW p.767 col.1: 'bhairava mf(ā and ī)n. (fr. bhīru) frightful, terrible, horrible, formidable, MBh.; R. &c.' and 'm. N. of a form of Śiva'. The Purāṇas list 8 Bhairavas: mahā-, saṃhāra-, asitāṅga-, ruru-, kāla-, krodha-, tāmracūḍa- or kapāla-, and candracūḍa- or rudra-Bhairava. Other senses: 'a jackal', 'a mountain', 'N. of a Rāga'. The root words: MW p.758 'bhīru mf(ū or u)n. fearful, timid, cowardly, afraid of', from √bhī 'to fear, be afraid of'. MW p.747 'bhaya n. (√bhī) fear, alarm, dread'.
asanas.story_link_honest_wording: This is the strongest WORD link to fear of the eight. SAY: 'Bhairavasana is named after Bhairava, Shiva's fierce form. Monier-Williams says the word bhairava means "frightful, terrible" and comes from bhīru, "fearful", from the same root as bhaya, "fear". Fear is built into the pose's name.' I checked no story that links this pose to fear, so treat it as a word fact only. FLAGS: do not use the usual origin myth in which Bhairava cuts off Brahma's fifth head. It is violence between gods and could offend. Never present Bhairava as a scary meme or a joke. Most followers will not know this Advanced A pose, so explain it in a line.

asanas.name: Garudasana
asanas.series: Not in the Ashtanga syllabus. It is absent from the ashtangayoga.info Primary, Intermediate and Finishing charts I opened, and from the Advanced A and B lists (grimmly modern and 1974 syllabus). It is an Iyengar (Light on Yoga) and general hatha pose. The closest Ashtanga pose is Vatayanasana (Intermediate), which has a similar wrapped-arm shape but a different name (vātāyana, 'horse').
asanas.sanskrit_word_meaning: MW p.348 col.3: 'garuḍa m. (√2. gṝ, Uṇ. iv, 155, "devourer", because Garuḍa was perhaps originally identified with the all-consuming fire of the sun's rays), N. of a mythical bird (chief of the feathered race, enemy of the serpent-race, vehicle of Viṣṇu, son of Kaśyapa and Vinatā; shortly after his birth he frightened the gods by his brilliant lustre; they supposed him to be Agni, and requested his protection; when they discovered that he was Garuḍa, they praised him as the highest being, and called him fire and sun, MBh. i, 1239 ff.'. MW does not say 'eagle'; 'eagle pose' is the yoga-book English name.
asanas.story_link_honest_wording: Don't call it an Ashtanga asana. If you need it, SAY: 'Other yoga styles have an eagle pose named after Garuda.' Garuda does appear in the checked ṭiṭṭibha fable: the robbed birds go to Garuda, and he takes their case to Vishnu (Ryder; Tawney). So he can be a character in the Tittibhasana reel without needing his own pose. MW's note on the gods being frightened by newborn Garuda's brightness (MBh Adi Parva) is a possible 'fear of the unknown' angle, but I did not open the MBh passage. FLAGS: avoid the Garuda-against-serpents conflict.

asanas.name: Hanumanasana
asanas.series: Advanced A (Third series): after Ganda Bherundasana, before Supta Trivikramasana.
asanas.sanskrit_word_meaning: MW p.1288 col.1: 'hanu-mat m. "having (large) jaws", N. of a monkey-chief (one of the most celebrated of a host of semi-divine monkey-like beings ... Hanumat was held to be a son of Pavana or Māruta, "the Wind"; and is fabled to have assumed any form at will, wielded rocks, removed mountains, mounted the air, seized the clouds, and rivalled Garuḍa in swiftness of flight ...)'.
asanas.story_link_honest_wording: This pose IS named after Hanuman: the name is Hanumat + āsana, so 'named after' is honest here. The link to the leap is a modern explanation (Wikipedia cites a 2008 children's book), and the pose is not found in medieval hatha texts. Say 'the split recalls Hanuman's leap', not 'the ancient texts say'. CHECKED FEAR SCENE: Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda, cantos 64 to 66 (Griffith, Book IV). No monkey dares the jump. Angad asks who will 'from our weight of fear set free / The leaders of our band and me?'. 'The legions sat in mute despair.' Jambavan turns to the silent Hanuman: 'Why still, and silent, and apart, / O hero of the dauntless heart?' This is fear of a task that seems too big, until someone reminds you of your strength. FLAGS: AYBKK already used Hanuman and Surasa, which happens during this same leap, so this will feel like a repeat. Use it only as a short aside, not the main story. Angad is a prince and the mission leads to war, so keep both in the background.
